speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) I should like to direct a question to his parliamentary assistant. In view of the representations made by lobster fishermen of Northumberland-Miramichi and Gloucester for a ten day extension of the lobster fishing season in their sections of area 7B, will the parliamentary assistant advise the house if a decision has been reached in this connection?

speakeroldname: Mr. J. Watson MacNaught (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR EXTENSION OF LOBSTER SEASON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for having given notice of his intention to ask this question. Representations have been received from the areas mentioned by him, which are part of area 7B. Since those representations were received investigations have been carried out to see if it would be desirable to extend the season. Complete returns for the month of May indicate that the catch is up substantially over the same

period last year. For the counties of Gloucester, Northumberland and Restigouche the catch is up over 60,000 pounds as compared with the same month last year. Preliminary returns for the months of May and June would seem to indicate that the over-all catch for the season will be substantially higher than it was last year.
In addition, many fishermen have already taken in their traps and have started to catch other species of fish. If an extension were made at this late date I think considerable confusion would ensue both to the fishermen and to the processors. An extension into July would also mean that many lobsters which are moulting or have moulted already would be taken and this would result in heavy losses. For these reasons it was felt that it would not be desirable to extend the season and consequently no extension will be granted.

Mr. Chairman, this is the first item of the army estimates, and I had deferred comment in regard to certain matters in connection with the army until we had reached this point. In the first place I wish to deal with something that has already been under consideration, that is, a subject that was brought up by the minister himself under the general item and which it was not possible for him to deal with at the time it was brought up. If you will permit me, I shall wait for a moment, because it will be convenient to wait until the members have readjusted themselves to whatever position they want, inside or outside the house.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I must say that I can entirely agree with the comment just made by the Leader of the Opposition. It seems that we always have a certain amount of confusion in the committee immediately after the orders of the day are called. I would ask hon. members to co-operate in giving order to the first speaker as soon as possible.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to refer to a subject that was discussed before and which I think could be clarified as far as this house is concerned; that is, the situation in regard to the announcement of the retirement of the present chief of the general staff. Some attempt was made to create the impression that this had been suddenly raised, and I regret that amongst remarks which were put forward in a very courteous manner by the minister, he should have adopted a somewhat cheap and tawdry attitude in regard to this particular subject, when he imputed to me the thought that this had been brought forward simply as something to cause embarrassment to the government and then to be dropped. The remarks that I have made

Supply-National Defence stand. If there has been any embarrassment or misunderstanding, it was due to the way in which this was done. It was not I who first raised any question about this matter. The statement was given to the press at a time when, the minister well knows, considerable interest had been aroused because of other events. The statement was given to the press outside of the house, and very naturally the press called for comments in regard to this subject and were themselves already commenting on this subject before it was raised here.
I would point out that in no remark I made was there any suggestion of criticism of the press. The press dealt appropriately with the statement given to them. I recognize that in the ordinary course of events many of these statements are given direct to the press. I would point out that in this case, however, it was impossible that there could not be some particular interest in the public mind, and I should imagine very great interest in the minds of the members of parliament, in regard to the circumstances surrounding the senior positions in the army, the air force and the navy. It was impossible to escape the questioning that came from the press immediately in regard to this announcement. It was for that reason that I raised a question about the advisability of making a statement that manifestly must invite questioning on the way it was done. I indicated my belief that it would have been desirable to have it done inside the house. I still think that it would have been best to have done it in that way and that it would have avoided the very discussion which the minister deplores.
The minister brushed lightly over the suggestion there was any reason to make such an announcement here. Yet he had already established the practice only the day before in another case. Although the circumstances were entirely different, nevertheless it related to appointments within the armed service. I want to point out that since this matter was discussed further evidence has been given of the fact that this is not an ordinary procedure, that there is more to this matter, and that we are entitled to more information than has been given.
The chief of the general staff-and he is the chief of the general staff at this time- is recognized, outside of Canada as well as inside of Canada, as one of the most competent field officers who came out of the last world war in any army. His services at the age of 52 are still extremely valuable services, whether as chief of the general staff or in some other capacity. He has behind him years of training, years of experience and years of the most intimate knowledge of this

complex period in which we live. It is an open secret that it would have taken little in the way of suggestion by this government to have made his services available in some other capacity outside of Canada if not in Canada.
Not one of us, as a member of parliament, should disregard the fact that when a man has accumulated vast experience at the age of 52, we all have some interest in that accumulation of experience. If there is some post, either in Canada or outside of Canada, in the common cause in which we are all so deeply concerned, to which that skill can be directed, then it should be our interest that this be done. It is with that thought in mind that I would still hope that the government will reconsider the course which it apparently has followed and which we must assume it has followed unless there is any other explanation.
Since this matter was last discussed in this house there has been an announcement that an able and gallant officer employed in another service has had his period of service extended. There is no member of this house who has a higher regard or higher admiration for General Worthington than I have.
I for one greatly welcomed the announcement that at the age of 65 his period of appointment had been extended still further in the very important post he now occupies. It happens that I have known him intimately for many years, and my respect for him is based not only upon reputation but upon personal knowledge. I welcome the fact that he continues in the post which he now occupies, and a very difficult post it is. This fact merely indicates, however, that there is no automatic rotation on the basis of time of service which suggests that Canada must lose the services of those whose experience can be of value.
It may well be that the government does not think that the chief of the general staff should continue in that post. I simply submit again the earnest hope that reconsideration will be given to this subject, and point out that if he is not to be continued in service as chief of the general staff, there are other fields of activity in which that long experience can be employed to the advantage of the Canadian public. May I immediately say that this has nothing to do with any views he may have expressed or any particular aspect of his service as a soldier. It is agreed without exception by everyone who knows that in the field of military experience and military training this man stands high in the regard of our own armed forces and of the senior members of the armed forces of the other nations of NATO.

I would hope that at the very peak of his mental and physical ability we should find his services employed elsewhere. In emphasizing this point I would emphasize that there is an anomaly in the fact that we see a highly qualified soldier retiring at 52 and being replaced by another soldier, for whom we all have high regard, at the age of 58. All this raises questions in the minds of every one of us, questions based upon the value of the service that can still be performed, questions based upon the contradictions that the government itself has placed before us when it renews other appointments of men much senior in age and, without any reflection on any one of them, men who have certainly not gained higher recognition amongst the senior members of the armed services of other nations as well as our own.
I leave the subject there. I would hope that this would not become the basis of any attack on General Simonds or upon any other officer, nor that comments of this kind should be regarded as reflecting on any other officer. I have sought to bring the matter forward simply on the basis of the training that has been given to this man and the fact that for long years to come a pension wMl be paid of over $10,000 a year to a man whose life expectancy is 25 years at this time. I would think that, as a matter of good business and common sense, we should seek to employ his services rather than pay a pension of that kind without any immediate return from now on to the country which he has served so well.
I come back to the discussion of the army organization. I feel sure that all hon. members have read with interest in the past 24 hours of the moving of an engineering unit of some 300-odd men from western Canada to Gagetown by air transport. I point out that the transport squadron which has been carrying out this airborne movement is doing precisely the thing that we have already suggested should be regarded as the basis of the organization of a modern Canadian defence force. I hope there will be no confusion in the mind of any hon. member about our recognition of the fact that there are certain static units of a type that do not lend themselves to that type of organization. Certainly harbour defence units, heavy anti-aircraft batteries and other static units of that kind embraced in the general services of the army could not be brought within the scope of a reorganization of this type.
However, if we are going to ask ourselves the basic question, what must a Canadian unit be called upon to do in the light of the
Supply-National Defence declared purpose it now serves, then I suggest that large mass formations simply fail to comply with that demand. At the very outset we are told not only in the white paper but in the statements of the minister that we must now contemplate the possibility of direct attack upon Canada itself. If that is so, then the minister cannot be under any impression that on the scale of the warfare that would develop if that unhappy event should ever occur the number of men now trained as airborne troops would be in any way adequate for the immediate demands of such a war. If there is one warning that we have been given over and over again by those most competent to advise us in this respect it is that the major decisions in another war would be reached within a very short time, and that the best way for us to prevent that war happening is to have forces in being ready for immediate service, forces of a type that could be employed without delay to meet a situation of that kind.
We are witnessing at this very time the assembly of a division of the first Canadian division at Gagetown. On July 19 there will be a march-past of units which undoubtedly will be a tremendously impressive sight. Well trained men of the brigades of that division will march past in a way which will arouse the admiration, the respect and the confidence of all Canadians. But let us just remember that it is taking weeks to assemble those forces in Gagetown. Let us recall that all the plans for that assembly have taken some time to work out. Let us recall that there has been a great movement of ground transport. Let us realize that this single division has demanded an amount of time to bring it together which most certainly would not be available in the event of another outbreak.
The test of our strength in the collective NATO organization is the speed with which we can perform any duties we might be called upon to perform. Since an attack on Canadian soil is now regarded as almost inevitable in the event of a war of this kind breaking out, then I must repeat my plea that immediate and urgent consideration be given to the formation of compact units of conventional types but unconventional formations which, in combat teams suitable to movement by air transport, could be put down at strategic airfields through the north, which invariably are placed close to the critical points where trouble of this kind might occur. With only a few exceptions-and I concede immediately that there are notable exceptions- there are well-established airports near the danger points across the north. Therefore, with warning of impending danger, units

Supply-National Defence could be moved into position, if they were units of this type. It would however be impossible to improvise organization of this kind, training of this nature or the transport facilities essential for it in a matter of days or hours.
Then, if we came to an acceptance of the belief that we should organize a substantial part of our army on this basis of a strictly Canadian concept of combat teams, airborne, then we would ask ourselves whether that would fit into our partnership in NATO. Immediately the answer is given that we have commitments to NATO. I am not sure whether it is a brigade or a division, but I am rather inclined to think that it is a division. The minister said it was a division, but then qualified the statement afterwards when he was questioned upon it. If it is a division, then the government must tell us how it proposes to maintain that division; it is certainly not in a position to do so now. If it is a brigade, then that will be a relatively small formation in relation to the very large land formations which will soon be available in Europe, from the combined strength of West Germany, France, Belgium, Holland, Italy, Spain and the other NATO countries of Europe.
For that reason I think we may well assume that the NATO staff and the members of NATO welcome the organization in Canada of a unique force unparalleled in any other NATO country, a force which by its adaptability to our own particular requirements would be peculiarly suited to special requirements in different parts of the world where NATO, or associated bodies, might seek its assistance.
The expression has already been used in this debate that such a force could be compared to a fire brigade and that is exactly what it would be. Or perhaps it would be a combination of fire brigades to put out fires in spots where there might be trouble, either in Canada or at some distant point. If some difficulty broke out at some distant point in Europe, in Africa or in Asia, in which we had a concern, such as we have already shown in Korea and in Germany, then I feel sure NATO would welcome the fact that we would have these fire brigades which could be put down in a place to deal with that fire. No other country would have equally mobile units.
The question then arises as to the expense. It is only necessary to look at the number of aircraft we already have to realize that we have a very large accumulation of transport aircraft. Let us consider new methods of using those aircraft. There are ways in which they could be employed on a rental

basis that would give an actual return through the use of those aircraft at times they were not in service. In fact it would not be dissimilar to the method that was employed some years ago when our militia, artillery and cavalry were fully horsed and able to go to camp as complete units. Those horses were used throughout the year for ordinary farm and other activities. Then they were brought to camp, and the units were given training with the complete horse equipment. It may seem far-fetched to draw a comparison between horse transport and air transport. I suggest it is no more farfetched than the developments which have taken place since the days of the 12-pounder, or the 15-pounder, or the 18-pounder, as compared with modern atomic weapons.
We are moving with events so fast that our minds must be adjusted to those events. I would hope we might have some indication of a willingness on the part of the government to expand the very type of organization which a flight, which took place only yesterday, demonstrated can be done so satisfactorily. That however was only with a single unit in a single branch of the service. Multiply that by all the conventional units required. 'And if the minister asks, "How would you work this out?" I would suggest a very normal and proper method. There is now a transport squadron of the R.C.A.F. with heavy transport machinery. Take that transport squadron and find out how many men in combat teams of infantry, artillery, armour, engineers and other essential services could be moved quickly by that transport squadron. Then you would establish your basic combat team formation in relation to your present air transport squadron, then convert some of your present transports. We have transports now that could be sold for commercial service, and we could acquire the type of transport known as the flying boxcar, and other similar transport machines required for these particular services.
Instead of this involving great added expense, I am satisfied we would greatly reduce the expense of our army organization and have an infinitely more effective force than we can have so long as we continue to retain the present organization of our permanent force and our militia. May I point out that it has never been questioned that the real backbone of our defence organization is the militia, whether it be the army, the air force or the navy. The feeder to the permanent force, the organization which stimulates interest in the permanent force, is the militia force. It is the training of these militia units much more than any advertising, more than any appeal by radio, or more than any appeal of

that kind which puts in the minds of young Canadians the thought of service in our armed forces.
Even if we have some airborne units at present in the permanent force we still have not extended to the militia the backbone of our whole defence organization, this modern concept of defence organization. The remarks I make in regard to a reorganization upon a concept of that type apply to the militia and I repeat once again that the way in which we shall best arouse the interest that will provide the manpower for these forces is to give to these forces the appearance of reality, the sense of reality, which has been lacking in a substantial part of our militia training. If anybody is in doubt about that, let him talk to rpilitia officers with pre-war experience who are still continuing their services in the militia. They will tell him that they have not been having the competitive practices that were such a stimulating part of the training in the years before the first and second world wars.
In so far as the training is concerned, give to the young men the idea that they are part of a unique Canadian force, and the justifiable pride of Canadians in their own country will assert itself in an increased interest in participation in those organizations.
There is another reason why Canadians of all people in the world should be thinking in terms of airborne forces. We need not have any sense of false modesty. There is something about the life in this large land of ours, something about the spirit of our youth, which lives so much in the open air, which has given our people special adaptability to air transport, to air service and everything connected with air development. In the first world war Canadians were supreme amongst all the armed forces of the world. In the second world war they continued that great tradition, and our great bush pilots of the north followed that tradition with equal valour and with tremendous success in the years of peace. With this tradition behind us we Canadians have the adaptability, have the spirit, have the natural qualification for this type of service. I do appeal to the minister to give us a picture of a positive plan for the use of the army which is certainly still lacking.
We have had a statement in the white paper which is really wholly uninformative as to any real developments in the future. I would point out that in Britain when their white paper was presented a few months ago positive statements of policy were enunciated which gave to their people confidence that the military staff was approaching the future 50433-3474
Supply-National Defence * with open vision. It was laid down as a positive statement of policy in the white paper in Britain that naval ships were now primarily regarded as bases for guided missiles. There is nothing in our white paper to tell us that already there has been a change in the attitude toward the artillery; that no matter how long it may be, the concept is now changing to the idea of an artillery weapon being a platform for guided missiles. The period of transition will be long, but already, through having seen the dummy that was included in the parade here not long ago, we know that the guided missile is contemplated here in Canada and actually is being experimented with and being used. It is a matter of common knowledge, and no secret, that the Canadian artillery has already fired a guided missile as a part of artillery training.
Why not challenge the imagination of the people of Canada by stating that the concept of the Canadian artillery is already in a transitional period from the conventional weapon to the guided missile, land to land, land to air, as well as air to air? Tell them also that, while the guided missile may become the most important weapon of the artillery, with certain obligations we have and certain essential demands, there will still be the conventional rifle weapon for certain specific services. None of this is yet given. Give to us the picture. Give to Canadians a challenge to their imagination and they will respond to that challenge.
As far as the navy is concerned, give us the broader picture there. As far as the air force is concerned, they definitely are in the future from the point of view of guided missiles, air to air and air to land.
We are on the army part of the estimates, Mr. Chairman. I submit that unless there is more than we have yet been told, a great deal more, then there is a lack of co-ordination and planning in regard to the army, which should be a cause of concern to every hon. member. I hope that the minister will indicate not only his willingness to approach this whole subject with an open mind, but also that instructions will be given to his planning staff to seek a strictly Canadian type of airborne organization, with compact, hard-hitting combat teams which could be moved to any distant point of the great Canadian north and be available also to NATO for such service as might be part of our common defence.
I submit that in relation to this suggestion there need be no question that NATO would gladly revise its arrangements to embrace within this combined organization a great modern military organization of this type.

Mr. Chairman, before we leave this item I should like to take a few minutes to emphasize once again the need for an integrated program of ideological training for our armed services. When I was organizing my thoughts on this subject I was beset by the usual temptation to cover the subject in some detail and to prepare a speech that would attract attention and look well in Hansard. But an ideology is a quality of life. It is not something merely to be talked about; it is something to be lived out in our daily lives.
We all realize that time is always precious. To members of parliament in the closing days of the session it is doubly so. There is also the uncomfortable fact that every unnecessary word, every minute wasted in this house, is also a waste of the taxpayers' money. Consideration of these facts drove me to the conclusion that I would not be living out my personal ideology if I did not endeavour to compress into five or six minutes what I would normally require 15 or 20 minutes to say. I assure hon. members that I would not take even these few minutes were I not absolutely convinced that this is a matter of urgent and vital importance. I say that for three reasons.
The first reason is that we are now living in an ideological age. We may not like it; we may not accept it; but nevertheless it remains a fact and we cannot alter it. For concrete proof we need only to examine the impact which the very word communism has today on our thinking and on our everyday lives.
My second reason is the experience of the United Nations soldiers in the Korean war. In former wars when a soldier was taken prisoner the war was over as far as he was concerned, but the United Nations soldiers who were taken prisoner in Korea found that the war was not over for them; in fact it was just beginning. The conflict in which they found themselves involved was ideological. I am not going to take time to elaborate on this point; instead I refer hon. members to a booklet published by the British defence ministry entitled "Treatment of British Prisoners of War in Korea". The fact to remember is that in future wars the prison camps must be regarded as battlegrounds in the war for men's minds and souls.
My third reason is that the continuous stockpiling of nuclear and thermonuclear weapons, together with the means of delivering them over long distances, must inevitably lead to a stalemate where neither side can afford to risk a shooting war. The recent change in the tactics and strategy employed

by the rulers of Soviet Russia indicate that they accept this position of armed stalemate as a fact, but there is not the slightest indication that the men of the Kremlin have abandoned their objective of communist world domination. They have not forgotten their past ideological victories which enabled them to gain control of whole nations without firing even a single shot. Therefore as the likelihood of a shooting war decreases it is reasonable to assume that the ideological war will be intensified.
These facts have great significance and far-reaching implications. They call for cold, realistic appraisal and for immediate and effective action. Here I feel it is necessary to point out that we should never confuse ideological training with a program of information and education. There is a vast difference between the two. We must at all costs avoid the mistake of trying to substitute one for the other.
I know that some provision is made for group discussion as a part of military training. As one who has had considerable experience with group discussion, both with service personnel and civilians, I know that it can serve a useful purpose; but only if it leads to decision. Endless discussion without leading to any decision is futile.
An ideology is an idea in action, an idea that is out to change the world. Ideas in action imply decision. President Eisenhower stressed this fact when speaking to the West Point graduating class on June 11 of this year when he said:
Change is inescapable in human society. Since the beginning of history the quality of a nation has been measured by its capacity to meet and master these evolving circumstances. The capacity of man has been gauged, in part at least, by his flexible adjustment to the new and novel, without sacrifice of principle or abandonment of standards. But change in the leisurely days of the past was gradual and evolutionary. Now, within a single generation, a natural process has become a cataclysmic rush.
Mr. Peter Howard, a noted British author, voiced the same thought in a recent broadcast. Perhaps I should explain that Mr. Howard is a full-time member of moral rearmament and he is now accompanying a mission of 60 statesmen which is visiting the national capitals of Asia and the Middle East at the invitation of their national governments. This mission is headed by Mr. Ole Bjorn Kraft, the leader of the Danish Conservative party who was formerly foreign minister and chairman of NATO. When broadcasting from Taipei, Formosa, Mr. Howard had this to say:
We live in an age of hope and danger. The hope is that millions today are resolved to build a new kind of world. The danger is that, frustrated by delays and disappointments, or lured by promises or fears of false leadership, some nation may

resort to atomic force in an effort to enforce its will upon mankind and so destroy the world as we know it. We need a vast transformation of human society-and it can happen fast.
Those two speakers stressed two essential facts which we must grasp. The first is that change is inescapable and the second is that change in our social order will be brought about by one of two world forces. The world of the future will be shaped either by the communist ideology or by a positive democratic ideology. These are the two alternatives and we should be thankful that there is an alternative to communism. Otherwise there would be no hope for the world.
If the world is to be shaped by a positive democratic ideology we must start at once to develop that ideology and put it into effect. To do that we must have a program of ideological training for everyone, and for the reasons already stated the armed forces are the logical place to begin.
Referring to our defensive regional pacts at San Francisco on June 24, and replying to the charges made by Soviet foreign minister Molotov, our minister of external affairs said:
Our unity in this regard cannot be shaken by untrue and unwarranted allegations that such arrangements are aggressive and provocative. We know that they are not and we will not abandon them. They are a shield against aggression itself and from any state. We will not-we dare not- abandon them until our security can be assured on a broader, better basis by the United Nations- or until peace rests on something even stronger than force of any kind.
I suggest that the "something even stronger than force of any kind" is a positive democratic ideology. It cannot be anything else. The essence of this ideology is an idea great enough to unite humanity. This idea is moral change. Everyone changes; the communists change; the capitalists change; the whites change and the blacks change. The east can change and the west can change. Then they can all unite in remaking the world by living a quality of life based on absolute moral standards. Then and not till then will true peace be realized.
Our minister of external affairs emphasized this point when addressing the United Nations tenth anniversary session at San Francisco on June 26-just a few days ago. He said:
There will be no peace until national policies are based on the U.N. charter-above all until we live our own lives in accordance with its principles.
This brings it right down to the level of each individual and points up the need for absolute moral standards. There can be no democratic ideology without absolute moral standards, because the ideology that changes communists must be a moral force in action.
Supply-National Defence Trained communists are quick to realize that a moral standard must be absolute; otherwise it is not a standard at all.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I should like to quote a few more words from Mr. Howard's broadcast to which I referred earlier. Later on in this broadcast to red China he used these words:
Attempts, however sincere, to make a new world must inevitably fail unless a new type of man is created to live in it. New systems crumble before the same old motives of greed, mistrust and exploitation. Those who use hate to gain control inevitably find that they have to use force to keep it. You cannot make a new world out of the same old people. You cannot make a good omelette out of bad eggs. A new type of world demands a new type of man. The ideology which produces the new type of man will win the world.
I could continue at some length, Mr. Chairman, but I think I have already said enough to make my point. I draw this need for an integrated program of ideological training to the attention of the Minister of National Defence and through him to his colleagues in the cabinet, the chiefs of staff and all others who are responsible for the training of our armed services. I know that some thought has already been given to this matter, but I believe the time has come when we must crystallize our thoughts and translate them into positive action.

Mr. Chairman, I hope my hon. friend will forgive me for descending from the high spiritual plane to which he has exalted us to the more mundane level on which I have my existence. I should like to ask a question of the Minister of National Defence. What licences are paid for by the army for its transport drivers to the various provinces of Canada?

I understand that with regard to the registration of vehicles we have arrangements with all the provinces whereby we pay a nominal sum that takes care of the cost of the plate and clerical expenses. Those arrangements vary to some degree in the different provinces, but in no province do we pay the full normal registration fee for the vehicle, as do civilians.

Every
province is paid in some form, either for the trucks or for the drivers?

Yes; it is done by agreement between our department and the province concerned. My remarks were addressed to the registration of vehicles. In respect of drivers, we also have arrangements with the provinces. In some cases we pay for the licence and in some cases we make other payments in lieu. We have varying arrangements with the different provinces.

Supply-National Defence
Could the minister tell me in which provinces the payments are made for licences?
I have not that information here, but I shall be glad to get it for the hon. member.
Does your department pay gasoline tax to the provinces?
There are varying arrangements about that. I can obtain that information.

Perhaps the minister could get a little more detailed information. Just to say that there are varying arrangements does not give us very much information. Perhaps the minister could get us the detailed information in regard to each of the provinces respecting the vehicle licences, the drivers' licences and the gasoline tax. There are those three questions.
I should be very glad to get the information.

Mr. Chairman, the subject of the army in general is of intense interest to a great many members of this house and the people of Canada. I am not sure that in the course of the minister's remarks on June 16 and 17 he dealt with the army as fully as he might. I have been looking back at the record and endeavouring to fill in the gaps that escaped my memory. I find that the minister hurried over the army, so it seems to me, in the course of his remarks.
When he was replying to us on June 16 he gave a rather short statement-not that that was any new experience for me. With the former minister of national defence I was accustomed to being ignored completely or else brushed aside with just a very short answer. The present minister was somewhat more amenable to argument. When I was discussing the armoured corps, and particularly the armoured personnel carrier, he said I had almost persuaded him to look at it closely again. I am not going to deal now with that particular problem of the armoured personnel carrier but I want to ask the minister to give his attention to the armoured corps in general.
Last year I spoke on this matter at considerable length and marshalled all the arguments that came to my mind. As a result I entertained a faint hope that this year, with a new minister in charge, perhaps the armoured corps might receive the recognition that it deserves. To my disappointment, however, the Royal Canadian Armoured Corps was brushed aside by the present minister

in a phrase which is to be found at page 4863 of Hansard, a few lines from the top. That phrase is "together with supporting armour". That is all the minister could find to say with regard to the Royal Canadian Armoured Corps.
This is an astonishing decline in one of the great arms of the service. The Royal Canadian Armoured Corps is the lineal descendant of the cavalry; and the cavalry over a long period of time occupied an important position in the army. I am not suggesting that the armoured corps is of greater importance than is the infantry corps, the artillery or the engineers. An army is composed of groups of supporting arms which must work together in order to achieve success. But when the Minister of National Defence is dealing with the army in general, I think he should give due recognition to one of the great branches of the army and that he should not dismiss it in a phrase such as "supporting armour".
The minister might have mentioned the regiments which now are equipped with armoured fighting vehicles. He might have indicated their role other than, as it appears here, just simply in a supporting role to the infantry. He might have named the regiments but he did not do so.
Last year I was advocating that it was absolutely essential, in a modern army fighting with conventional weapons, that the armoured corps be maintained. We cannot ignore conventional weapons. The minister does not do that. As reported at page 4863 of Hansard he says this:
Our own best military advice and the advice of the highest military chiefs of NATO is that the need for ground forces of the highest calibre will be continuing and urgent throughout the foreseeable future.
We must not be misled by the tremendous threat of nuclear weapons entirely to ignore conventional weapons. Even at the present time when disarmament matters are being considered, no one has suggested the complete disbandment of the armed forces. If minor wars break out conventional weapons will be used as they have been used within recent years; and if you are going to use conventional weapons you must surely, in these days, have armour.
The history of the development of the tank is an extremely interesting one. It took years for people to understand the value of it. Even in the opening years of the second great war there was great misunderstanding as to the importance and the value of the tank; and I regret that, since that war, there seems to be a misunderstanding in Canada of the value of that particular type of armoured fighting vehicle.

As I pointed out last year, we have evolved a very efficient, highly-trained infantry fighting force, with artillery and engineers. They have had great experience in the course of the Korean war. They have had plenty of field experience in exercises in Europe with the NATO forces. But during all this period since the conclusion of the second great war, armour has been neglected. I advocated-as did others on this side of the chamber-that our contribution to the NATO forces in Europe should be armour and not infantry. The former minister would not consider that suggestion. The present minister says this, and I quote from page 4863 of Hansard:
Within the NATO system the role of the Canadian army is primarily, of course, an infantry role.
Why "of course, an infantry role"? I recall asking a year or two ago why our commitments to NATO should have been infantry and I think the answer was that that was what we were requested to supply. 1 am obliged to accept at their face value statements such as that made in the house, but I wonder whether that was not what we suggested we might supply. If that was the case, I think our suggestion was wrong. There are millions of men available on the continent of Europe to supply ground forces in an infantry role whereas the more specialized mechanized forces might well be produced here in Canada and trained with the NATO forces overseas. My suggestion last year and the year before was that our NATO commitment might better be a brigade of tanks, with a brigade of tanks at home in Canada to effect the necessary rotation of regiments. Had that been done or were it done now the Royal Canadian Armoured Corps would be as important a force within the Canadian army as it was during the second world war.
I went on to point out the great importance, with regard to an army, of the training of senior officers and that they are severely handicapped if they are not given troops of all arms to work with. How can an infantry commander of the rank of general, commanding a division or a corps, make use of armour if he has none to deal with? How will the infantry battalion commanders learn to work with tanks if there are none to work with? The result is that in the actual higher command of the Canadian army there must, of necessity, these last few years be a lack of training in the use of armour.
That is not the case with regard to the army of the United Kingdom. The United Kingdom is maintaining in the NATO forces a substantial contribution of armoured divisions. The United States is not neglecting its
Supply-National Defence armoured corps nor is Russia. Why Canada should be doing this is something that I do not understand. I do not understand why we should be just supplying infantry forces when we could have a combined fighting force of armour and infantry, with the artillery and the engineers, as we had in the second great war.
The tank has proved its usefulness ever since it was effectively brought out on the battlefield in the fall of 1917. Some misguided people who observed bogged down tanks in the first great war thought that they were completely useless. They were most effectively used in the fall of 1917, and again used effectively in the great campaigns of 1918, particularly from the 8th of August on.
Then you will recall that in the inter-war period the tank was neglected and came back into usefulness at the beginning of the second great war when the Germans so effectively overran Poland with an armoured force. Canada woke up to the problem after some considerable delay and produced tanks of her own which were not used on the battlefield as gun tanks. Finally she equipped her army with the necessary number of tanks to form armoured brigades and armoured divisions. The striking force of the Canadian army in the second world war was immensely enhanced by virtue of that fact. The striking force of the Canadian army at the present time is not nearly as strong as it should be because it is chiefly infantry. A balanced Canadian army cannot be produced under these conditions.
I would be interested to see what the manoeuvres will be during the immensely interesting training period that is now about to commence at Gagetown. To what extent will tanks be used in these manoeuvres? They will perhaps be used to as great an extent as is possible with two regiments, but there will be nothing in the nature of armoured brigade action or armoured division action. It will be a case of tanks supporting infantry. There will be press photographers there and I very much fear that in the closing days of the exercises at Gagetown we will see infantry going into action supported by tanks. Some of the infantry will be riding on top of the tanks, some will be walking behind the tanks and some will be walking along the ground with the tanks out on the flanks. This will be supposed to be a first-class infantry action with tanks, overlooking the fact that all the men on the ground could easily be cut down by machine gun fire, mortar fire and high explosive shells without the least trouble in the world. That will be the type of infantry plus tank action that I suppose will be produced in the exercises this summer.

From the size oi the Gagetown area I judge that tank manoeuvres could be held there with the greatest of ease. Its terrain is suitable for that purpose, and I think the training of armoured formations could very-well be carried on there. If we could get back to a balanced Canadian army with its proper component of tanks we would have a much better striking force than at the present time. A force of that nature could be used along the lines that have been advocated in the house by the Leader of the Opposition and by the hon. member for Es-quimalt-Saanich. We could have an airlifted striking force because it is possible nowadays to provide planes with the carrying capacity to transport tanks.
The tank is not out of the picture so far as present-day conceptions of warfare are concerned, but the tank is out of the picture so far as the Minister of National Defence is concerned because he does not even bother to mention it. He had nothing to say about the Royal Canadian Armoured Corps. It is for that reason I am making this protest now. I think the minister will have to adjust his thinking with regard to the Canadian army. He will have to engage in consultation with his advisers and suggest to them that a balanced Canadian army is the requirement for the present day. I grant that we have first-class infantry, artillery and engineers and give full credit to them. I think they are very highly trained. As I pointed out last year, when you consider the rotation that has gone on in Europe and the number of brigades that served in Korea, we have trained scores of senior officers, majors, lieutenant-colonels and brigadiers, in actual warfare in Korea or in simulated warfare in the exercises in Europe. We have also trained artillery officers and engineers.
The result is that there is available in army circles a highly trained group of officers of the rank of major, lieutenant-colonel or brigadier in those services. What officers of that rank have you in the armoured corps? The armoured corps has become, as I said before, the Cinderella of the Canadian army. What officer from the armoured corps is likely to receive promotion and advancement? Their numbers are too few. Has any lieutenant-colonel of the armoured corps received active service training since the second world war or simulated active service training in Europe with the NATO forces? Of course not. The command for any armoured corps grouping has only carried the rank of a major and, so far as my information goes, no major has even exercised a squadron in its entirety. They have


been handed out by dribs and drabs. After all these years here is the Canadian army highly trained and very efficient in one respect and neglected in the other.
I do not wish to leave the impression that the two regiments comprising the armoured regiments of the Canadian army are not highly trained within their regimental duties. I do not want to leave that impression. I think they are both efficient regiments, but they have not had the advanced training that has been made possible for other units in the Canadian army. We are not drawing officers for higher positions from the armoured corps unless they are men whose experience extends back to the second world war. I am thinking now of the years ahead of us. If the present Canadian army set-up is continued, then 20 years from now there will not be an officer of high rank who has had any real experience in the use of armour. I think that is quite wrong.
At the beginning of the second world war and for several years thereafter it was bad enough dealing with high ranking officers who had no understanding whatsoever of the use of armour. At this late stage after the second world war I can perhaps express myself with some feeling on this matter, and possibly I might be a bit unkind to some of the high-ranking officers of the second world war. Perhaps they did not have the opportunities, but certainly it was difficult for them to understand how armour should be used. We had plenty of trouble during that war until experience was gained. Let us not go through that again. Let us develop a balanced Canadian army so that all officers of senior rank may have the same type of training. That is my protest to the minister. He neglected to say anything about armour in the course of his remarks. Not much was said about it in the white paper. I notice this at page 42:
The regular force Is now equipped with the British Centurion tank. A British type of armoured scout car has also been issued to regular units.
In view of the discussion we have had in other years with regard to the equipment of the armoured corps, I think the minister might well have elaborated on this and told us the complete equipment of the present active regiments. He might have told us about the equipment for the militia regiments within the armoured corps, and let the house know whether they are fully equipped with Centurion tanks, or whether a new type of tank is under consideration. He might have informed us, too, about this British armoured car, and perhaps the Minister of Defence Production might have

asked for extended powers to produce a Canadian armoured car. I believe that is within his field.
Unless the Royal Canadian Armoured Corps is revived and put back into its proper place in the Canadian army we will continue to have an ill-balanced fighting force, so far as the army is concerned.

Mr. Chairman, I should like for a few moments to deal with the request by the Canadian Girl Guides Association for the use of Connaught rifle ranges in Ottawa for the purpose of establishing a camp. I understand the request was made in March of this year by the association to the Minister of National Defence for the use of Connaught ranges in either July or August of 1957, for the purpose of holding an international girl guide camp under the auspices of the world association of girl guides.
As the minister indicated earlier, when the question was raised upon calling the orders of the day, this request has been made far in advance, and it is recognized that this is a rather long time ahead to make such a request. I think however the reason must be obvious to everybody including the minister. It takes a great deal of arrangement to make plans for a conference of this size, which will be attended by people from Europe, South America, Asia, Australia and New Zealand. Indeed, they come from all over the world to this conference. In addition, while the conference itself would last only ten days or two weeks, it is the desire of the Girl Guides Association of Canada to arrange other programs for the entertainment of the visitors so that they could visit Niagara, Banff and other points in Canada.
The girl guides association is not asking for money; apparently they have their own sources and can make the necessary financial arrangements. But a conference of this kind does require a great deal of organization and arrangement, with the result that requests for accommodation have to be made well in advance. As a matter of fact, I have been advised by the association that if a decision one way or another cannot be reached by the middle of this summer the whole plan will have to be scrapped, because it is impossible to make the arrangements on shorter notice.
The request has been made for the use of the ranges in either July or August. While the actual conference would take only ten days or two weeks the association would require the use of the grounds for perhaps a week before for purposes of preparation, and a week after to clean up the area. All told, it would take about a month.
Supply-National Defence
I am told that, on the advice of one of his senior staff officers, who shall be nameless, the minister has turned down the request, and that the staff officer has advised that the date is too far in advance, and that the request cannot be considered at the present time.
My advice is that the Connaught ranges are not used for matters connected with vital national defence. There is little doubt that if between now and 1957 the international situation should worsen to the point where war, or something approaching war, might be expected, the whole thing would be called off anyway. At the present time the Boy Scouts Association of Canada have the use of Camp Niagara at Niagara Falls, which is a military camp, where a great deal of training takes place. My advice is that Connaught ranges are not used in the same way as the camp at Niagara.
It has been said that the attempt to make arrangements is too far ahead and that the department is not in a position to say what might take place at Connaught ranges at that time. It seems to me that this is a stronger argument favouring the request, because it will be known two years in advance that the ranges would be occupied in July or August of 1957, and the department could make the appropriate arrangements.
Someone might ask why some other place should not be used, because there are, indeed, other places in Canada. This point has been investigated thoroughly by the association and they feel there is no other place suitable. Their chief reason for saying this is, of course, that other places such as Camp Niagara have not the suitable sanitary facilities for a conference of this kind.
Another important point is that in an international affair of this kind, while the boy scouts are at Niagara Falls, nevertheless this is the national capital and it would seem suitable that young people from other countries who visit Canada should have the opportunity to attend a camp located in the federal district near the national capital. I think the reasons are obvious, without further elaboration.
My understanding is that in the past the girl guides have had the use of Connaught ranges. I believe they were located there no more than two or three years ago when they established a national camp. Apparently there was no objection on that occasion. In this instance it is to be an international camp, and it seems to me the reasons for having it at Connaught ranges are obvious. There would be considerable prestige for Canada, and it would do a great deal to improve international understanding, and at virtually
5502	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence no cost to the government. Indeed, in my opinion it would do much more to create international good will than a lot of the money spent by the Department of External Affairs from time to time in various forms of entertainment.
Here is a great opportunity for young Canadians to learn what the young people of other places in the world are like, and to learn about their problems. It must be remembered that the young people who will be attending this conference are in many cases likely to be those who in future will be the leaders not only in Canada but in other countries. It cannot help but give them a good opportunity to learn our way of life, and it seems to me this is most important.
More than that, for our own young people it is a notable adventure in citizenship. They will have the opportunity to know better the young people from other parts of the world. I understand there would be anywhere from 12,000 to 20,000 in attendance, the great majority of whom would be Canadians. Nevertheless there would be several thousand from other parts of the world, in those places where girl guide and boy scout movements are in existence.
I hope the minister will reconsider the decision, for the reasons I have given. If the opportunity to hold the camp at Connaught ranges is turned down, or if some decision cannot be reached soon, there will be many thousands of young people in Canada who will be greatly disappointed. This would be a great pity. The advantages of holding the camp in the Ottawa area are many, from the long-range as well as from the immediate point of view. It would seem a pity if this venture is scuttled on the advice of a brass hat. It is not as though the association were asking for an assignment to them of a military area of great importance such as the camp at Petawawa, at Camp Borden or at Gagetown. They are asking for the Connaught ranges which the Dominion of Canada Rifle Association uses from time to time, and I am told the local militia also uses it occasionally for shoots. I can see no reason why appropriate arrangements could-not be made to let the association have it in 1957 for this purpose. As I say, they have had it before. The department permitted the boy scouts to use Camp Niagara, which is considerably more important than the Connaught ranges, I would think.
The Prime Minister himself, and certainly the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, are very interested in young people. If the Minister of National Defence does not see fit to let the association use Connaught ranges, perhaps the Prime Minister or the Minister 

of Citizenship and Immigration might assist the Girl Guides Association in finding other suitable quarters with proper facilities for young girls.
As I said before, this is a very worthy effort on the part of the Girl Guides Association of Canada. It will enhance the reputation of our young people at home and abroad. I do hope the minister will reconsider the matter before long; otherwise, it will have to be dropped.

Mr. Chairman, I want to back
up what the hon. member for Oxford has said about complying with the request of the Girl Guides Association for the use of the Connaught ranges. I think it is a great compliment to Canada that this fine association is having this world meeting here. It is a grand chance for Canada to show off a little, to give those people an idea of what Canada looks like and particularly of our hospitality.
If the Girl Guides Association, which is playing host to these fine young people from all over the world, considers that the Connaught ranges would be the best place possible for this camp, then the government should do everything possible not to put obstacles in their way, but to comply with their request. The hon. member for Oxford has said that these ranges have been used before by this same association. It is not something new. If they have used this site before, then obviously the association knows that the facilities are satisfactory and that they consider, after a great deal of thought, -I am sure they put a great deal of thought into this matter-that this would be the best possible place for the meeting to be held.
For a senior army officer to put obstacles in the way of this fine association is to me simply stupidity. It is a sample of bureaucratic stupidity. Simply to say that this is not a military organization; that there would be a little trouble and they might have to make some arrangements; that it is a little out of the normal course to do this thing, therefore we just say no, to me is just bureaucratic stupidity.
To use the words of an hon. member, I was in the army, and I have had lots of experience with this same kind of bureaucratic stupidity. I hope that the minister will give this serious consideration. This is an important matter. I do not know of any two finer organizations in the world than the boy scouts and the girl guides. They have given this thing serious consideration, and if they feel that Connaught ranges is the best possible site for their meeting, then I should think the government would fall over itself to comply with their request and

back up a fine organization of this kind instead of snubbing them and saying no, we are just not going to let you have this area, you can find some place else.
I urge the minister to reconsider this decision, apd I hope that before this debate is over he will be able to tell the committee and the Girl Guides Association that their very reasonable request will be complied with.

speechtext: Is there any further discussion on the army, regular and general?

Yes, Mr. Chairman. I do not intend to make any speech about it but I have a few questions I should like answered by the minister. In the army items on page 231 we notice an item set aside for professors and instructors at the Royal Military College. I understand there has been a pretty well complete integration as far as officer cadet training of all three services at the tri-service schools is concerned. I wondered whether the minister had taken any note of the action of the Royal Canadian Air Force Association at their last meeting when they requested that we return to the old system of having schools for each of the army services?

Yes, we have examined the resolution passed by the Royal Canadian Air Force Association and also our policy in relation to tri-service colleges. As the hon. member said, we have integrated the three services in each of the three colleges. We feel that that is desirable and advantageous, and we propose to continue having all of the colleges tri-service.

Further than that, we have been talking about integration all along the line. In connection with the services, will the minister outline what steps have been taken, if any, in connection with the training of staff officers at the staff college, to bring together the officers of the three services? Has any attempt been made along that line, to train them at one school, or at least in all three schools for all three services?

The national defence college is tri-service, as the hon. member knows, and the three service colleges are tri-service. In the air force staff college and the army staff college there are sprinklings of officers from the other services, so that while the staff colleges are predominantly for the service to which they are attached, there is some intermingling of personnel in the national defence college.

I might suggest to the minister that serious thought be given
Supply-National Defence in the future to more than just a slight intermingling of personnel at these schools. If we are to achieve the maximum effort out of the armed forces we must move steadily toward the goal of having staff people trained to understand completely the use and the effectiveness of the other arms of the services. As a matter of fact, we can safely say that here in Canada we cannot even begin to afford a miniature pentagon. The earlier that we can put together all three services in a combined force of some kind the better our defences will be. The minister will recall the words of General Pearkes, who said that the question of the type of uniform that was worn or its colour was not of great importance to him. From the staff point of view, probably very much more use of the great number of personnel in the various services could be made if real offensive steps were taken along the lines of integration; I mean by that, the requirements for personnel in the far north in connection with the D.E.W. line. In the first instance, this personnel may be members of the Royal Canadian Air Force for radar duty. It seems to me that at the same time the ground forces of the Royal Canadian Air Force might very well be trained in the very latest of infantry type weapons and their use so there will be no duplication by having to have the army as another branch of the service handle the actual protective work for radar personnel.
As a matter of fact, if that course were pursued we might be able to avoid the embarrassing situation we find ourselves in now where we are seeing United States servicemen on the streets of many of the northern cities and towns, which indicates that they are the people who are manning those radar defence lines. Perhaps we could make use of the ground personnel of the air force if they were trained in the use of the latest infantry weapons, given the same type of tactical training that is given to the infantry. We might then be in position to handle all the personnel requirements for our northern defence lines without having help from an outside country. I urge strongly to the minister that the first step to be taken would be to see that the staff colleges do more than just intermingle, that they start a program which will enable each one of them to understand completely the responsibilities of the others.
Coming down the list of items starting at page 321, I notice again an increase in the number of administrative officers. As I indicated once before, I think it is quite logical to expect an increase in the technical officers of the army and most certainly that would be indicated if we followed the advice of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre,

Supply-National Defence but I fail to see why there should be a steady increase of administrative personnel. I might go one step further and note that this is along the lines of the question I asked in connection with the navy.
I notice a fairly large increase in the number of office appliance operators employed by the army. This would indicate the utilization of modern office equipment and it should forecast a decline in the number of clerical workers who are mentioned on page after page. There seems to be no indication that the mechanization of office work is leading to any decrease in the number of routine administrative personnel. Could the minister give an indication why in each of these two instances we have increases in personnel at a time when the use of mechanical means might be decreasing that type of work?

Mr. Chairman, dealing first with administrative officers of which there is a slight increase in numbers: for some years it was found to be most difficult to obtain this type of officer and we were very short of them. The hon. member will recall that in his report on the engineering services Mr. Currie deprecated the lack of administrative officers. We have been making that up as fast as we can get suitable people of that category.
With regard to the office appliance operators, I may say that we are endeavouring to introduce as much mechanical type work as we can into the administrative side. The expectation is that as it becomes effective and these different steps are linked together we hope to be able to cut down somewhat on the clerical staff. We are in the transition stage at the moment.
I gather from the^ minister that we can hope to see some savings in that respect.
I would hope so.

I should like to refer again to the employment of architects. As far as naval architects are concerned,
I can understand that they might be used in the designing of ships or in connection with special work of that kind and therefore might require special training, but in connection with the construction of other types of buildings, even including hangars for the air force, I should like to know if any attempt has been made to integrate the services of the architects. Would it not be possible to have the architects operate from a central pool for all the armed services instead of each branch having its own group of architects?

Mr. Chairman, that is now being done; the architects of the three services 
are pooled. Of course in each service there are some specific types of work peculiar to that service and the duties of certain architects would follow that service line. Generally speaking, we are trying to use all architects in the most advantageous manner, which is, as the hon. member has suggested, by pooling them. It is working out quite well.

On page 328 the item for travelling and removal expenses is $19,127,000, whereas last year it was $16,397,000. The minister will recall that I asked for certain information in connection with removal costs for members of the armed services in Ontario and I found a return on my desk this morning. I have not had an opportunity to add this up, but it would seem to indicate at least 100 different moving companies. Could the minister give us any information as to what type of audit is made of this $19 million and of the utilization of approximately 100 companies in moving service personnel to and from Ontario? Is there any audit as to the cost involved, the time involved in moving, the merchandise or furniture that is moved and whether the actual removal is for straight military purposes?

The increase this year in travelling and removal expenses is due to the fact that the brigade now in Germany will be rotated and returned to Canada, which means a double movement of the outgoing brigade and the incoming brigade.
I might give the hon. member a statement as to how individual movements are handled, which I think is what he has in mind. When an officer or man is posted from one place of duty to another and is authorized to transfer his furniture and effects at public expense, it is the responsibility of his commanding officer to determine the most economical method of shipment and movement. It is the practice to call for at least two quotations and sometimes more in each case in order to get a competitive price. The officer or man who is being transferred then has the right to select the most economical of the tenders that have been received. If he exceeds the amount of the tender, then he must pay the added cost himself. In other words, there is a natural check in that way.
When the mover has been selected, he receives an order to move the furniture and effects. When the move has been completed, the moving company submits the invoice to the department including a certificate from the man that the services have been performed and the goods received. The officer who authorizes payment of the account must

also certify that the move was made under proper authority and that all charges are fair and just. In further support of the charges made, waybills, etc., are required to be submitted. These are used in checking on the sums involved. These procedures have been strengthened following some difficulties encountered last year, when there were some conspiratorial attempts to defraud.
The feeling of the departmental officials charged with this matter now is that, under the present system when a man is ordered to move, we have a fairly accurate and complete check on the cost of that movement. Of course, the cost of moving is pretty well established on a mileage basis, and there is usually not too much difficulty about that. The troubles we have had arose where a soldier conspired with a civilian. There were cases where movements had not been authorized or made and payments were made. It is as a result of this that we have tightened up the procedure and, so far as I know, it seems to be working satisfactorily.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Department of National Defence, resolution 236. At one o'clock the committee had been discussing the Canadian army, regular and general.

At one o'clock, Mr. Chairman, we were talking about questions of travelling and removal expenses and the minister had been outlining the method used to check these individual items. I wonder whether the minister might be able to tell us whether the department has any estimate as to the amount lost during the last fiscal year in connection with-and I think he used these words-attempts by conspiracy to defraud the department in connection with moving expenses. Can he tell us approximately how much the department has lost, whether any prosecutions were launched and whether there were any convictions?

As nearly as we can arrive at the figure involved, it is slightly over $9,000. Prosecutions were launched against 36 non-commissioned officers and men. Three were tried and convicted by general court-martial. One was sentenced to two years' imprisonment and one to 18 months' imprisonment and dismissal from Her Majesty's forces. One was fined $150 and severely reprimanded. Of the 21 who were tried by disciplinary courts-martial, 20 received disciplinary sentences, one with dismissal from
Supply-National Defence Her Majesty's forces, and one was acquitted. Of the 12 who were dealt with summarily and disciplined, one is being detained by the civil authorities on another civil prosecution.

Can the minister advise us whether any prosecutions were launched in this connection in the civil courts against any of the outside persons involved in connection with these travel and removal expenses?

The single civilian who was engaged in this business was prosecuted or at least his prosecution is pending-I do not think it has been completed-in the civil courts. When that matter is completed we propose to take civil action against him to recover such of the moneys as we can which were involved in the series of transactions.
I gather that only one civilian was involved in this matter and that it covers fairly well the complete amount which is involved in the loss of $9,000.

I think the facts will show that the man to whom I was just referring was the originator of a little system of his own and that he operated a moving business, at least ostensibly so. It was a local situation and it is being completely cleared up. It has already been cleared up as far as service personnel are concerned and is in a fair way to be concluded on the civilian side.

I see that, as shown at page 322, there is an increase in the number of accountants that are being employed by the army. I trust that they might be used in cases of this kind. I wonder whether the minister could inform us whether any audit check is made. He has outlined for us the procedure used in connection with the ordering of the civilian company to move the service personnel and how it is passed on by the commanding officer. Can the minister inform us whether any spot check is made by the department auditors or accountants of the actual invoicing made by the civilian companies to the army?

In the quartermaster general's department there are teams of accountants who go about the country, doing spot checks from time to time. These checks are followed by further and other spot checks by teams from the chief auditor's branch of the department. There are two series of checks which are being carried out all the time.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few comments following on the speech made this morning by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. I had rather hoped that the minister might answer his
5506	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence criticisms at once but that has not been done, and so I shall make my comments now.
I suppose it is no exaggeration to say that this job we are doing now is perhaps, in one sense, the most important job that we do all year because we are dealing with these vast amounts of money. I also take it that notwithstanding any misgivings we may have about the thermonuclear weapons, we are dealing with these estimates on the basis that what we have come to call the conventional army now must be regarded as worth while in itself and must be considered on its own basis.
We have had comments, notably from the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich and the Leader of the Opposition. I just quote one sentence from the speech of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich to be found at page 4870 of Hansard:
I do not believe in maintaining yesterday's establishments In order to fight the war of tomorrow.
In other words, there has been searching questioning as to the basis of our conventional army. This morning we had a speech by a man who I think we all concede has as good a right to speak on this subject as has any man in this chamber because he speaks of tanks, a matter in which he was at one time an expert and in which he has been desperately interested ever since, and on which he has spoken repeatedly in this House of Commons.
As I listened to him I confess that I was surprised. I have not followed military establishments as I should have but I was surprised to hear him say-as he did say-that our tanks had been neglected. That was the word he used. He repeated it. He described it in various ways. He gave instances. Then he went on to speak of what, of course, is a most important thing, namely the training of officers; and he said that senior officers had not had a proper chance. We all know what that means. He was sparing in criticism that I gather he could have made from what he had seen on the actual field of battle because of the fact that men in senior positions had not had the training in peacetime which they should have had. These warnings and others he has given us. Actually, as I listened to him, I could not help remembering another man of the same name who, 20 years ago, was trying hard to pierce the equanimity and lethargy of the British people; and we all know how dreadfully they suffered because he failed at that time, although he was much too magnanimous to harp on it afterwards.
I think that the speech made this morning demands the most searching and frank [Mr. Macdonncll.l

answer. I do not think it should be slurred over. Are these statements correct? It seems to me there are only three things the minister can do. There are really only two. First he could say that we should not take this too seriously because it is only the conventional army. I know he will not say that. The second thing he could say is that these criticisms are not valid. If he is going to say that, I suggest he has got quite a task on his shoulders in proving it. The third thing he could say is that these criticisms are valid and that he is going to take steps accordingly. If that is what he says, then I suggest it should not be left in the realm of vague generality but that he should try to convince us that he means business.
If none of these things is done, all I can say is that it seems to me that in dealing with these huge amounts we are not behaving like serious men but like children playing in the sand.

There is one question I should like to ask the minister. In discussing the navy the other day there was an item in the naval estimates for a total of 322 chauffeurs. In reply to questions at that time the minister said it was much less expensive to employ civilian personnel to do that work than to have service personnel do it. If that is the case, I wonder why there is no provision made in the army estimates for civilian chauffeurs. Apparently service personnel are used for this type of work in the army and the air force. If the argument the minister presented in favour of using civilian personnel in the navy applies, I am rather at a loss to understand why the same system is not used for the army and the air force.

I think the analogy between the services as put forward by the hon. member is hardly tenable. Incidentally, I might mention that at the bottom of page 326 of the estimates he will see that the army provides for 529 motor truck drivers. Generally speaking, however, the army service corps operates with military personnel. The army is a more mobile service than the navy which operates from fixed establishments.
