Truck and car driving in the army is different from driving in the other services. I think that will be readily understood. To a large extent, but not completely, we use army service corps personnel as drivers.

I follow the minister's remarks with respect to the army, but the air force is possibly a little closer analogy to the navy than the army. In addition, I should like to know whether the very large item of 529 motor truck drivers for the army includes

personnel who drive staff cars and that sort of thing at various defence establishments. I presume that is what the large number of chauffeurs and truck drivers are required for in the navy.

Can the
minister tell me what control the deputy minister has over army personnel and army policy?

As far as control over personnel is concerned, I think I must assume that responsibility and not the deputy minister. But the deputy minister is reasonably familiar at all times with the personnel situation and, in fact, has an assistant deputy minister who deals almost solely with civilian personnel. There is a chain of responsibility that goes up through the department and finally, like any other responsibility, rests on the minister's shoulders. I do not think I should demonstrate in detail how the whole chain works, but it is a comprehensive system of keeping control of the staff through the deputy minister, the assistant deputy minister, the director of personnel and various other branches of that part of the general administration.

Can the
civil administrative head interfere actively with the service heads of various departments and say that this shall be done in contradistinction to what they want done?

The position is that on the service side of each of the three services the chief of staff of the respective service and his officers are primarily responsible for the administration of personnel in that service. But senior officers, including the deputy minister and the chiefs of staff, confer with me with respect to the different service matters and matters on the civilian side from time to time. Generally speaking, however, internal arrangements with respect to personnel in any particular service rest with that service and the chief of staff of that service.
The permanent civil servant head really only has control of the non-service people in the department.
In detail, yes, that is so.

And the
army and the other services have complete control over their personnel.

Generally speaking that is true, but the minister is in control of the service personnel as he is of the civilian personnel. The deputy minister is also familiar with all aspects of the department,
Supply-National Defence but under normal circumstances the actual administration of a service is left to the chief
of staff and his officers.

I grant that the minister is responsible. He is responsible to the house and to the country. How many civilian personnel are there in the defence establishment over whom the deputy minister has actual control?

Generally speaking the
deputy minister exercises control, under my directions, of the civilian staff, which is approximately 50,000.
How many?

Approximately 50,000. He is concerned with their conditions of work, rates of pay, qualifications and other details, but from day to day the work is supervised by their immediate superiors and heads of branches. Therefore I think it would be fair to say that under me the deputy minister exercises a general control over all the civilian staff, and the detailed control is exercised by officials who in turn, of course, are responsible to him and through him to me.

What happens in a situation where the deputy minister believes that something should be done a certain way and the army staff decide it should be done another way? Is the matter then sent to the minister for decision?

I think it would depend, in large part, upon what the nature of the matter was. For example, if it had something to do with the firing of guns, or the provision of radar equipment for aircraft, or anything of an operational nature, the service view would obtain and it would be looked after by the responsible head of the branch concerned. But if it was a case of an amount of money to be spent for a certain type of radar equipment, or something of that kind, the service would make a study and would make a recommendation and ask for the necessary amount of money to be allocated to that purpose. But of course the deputy minister and I and financial officials on the civil side would look at the project carefully.
In other words, if it is an operational matter of a service, generally speaking we must rely upon the senior military officer in the particular branch of the service for advice. But if it is a question of finance or general administration, then naturally the deputy minister has to be consulted. He must be conversant with it, because the service and the civilian sides have to be integrated.
5508	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence
So it is a question I cannot answer categorically, but I hope I have made clear the division I have in mind.

There are a couple of matters about which I have spoken to the minister previously, and on which I would like to have information.
The first of these was the matter of the separated family allowance. The minister knows how that works, of course. One lives in Nova Scotia and is posted to Vancouver; and unless his wife and family are also moved to and located in Vancouver the separated family allowance does not apply. In other words you have to be together to be considered separated. I think it should be just the reverse, because in the case of a serviceman who goes into the service and has a home established where his wife and family are happy and comfortable, and then is posted out to the west coast or somewhere else, the wife and family are obliged to leave the home they have established and locate themselves in some other part of the country if they wish to qualify for the separated family allowance.
In many cases, where families have been moved in that way, they have found upon landing in Winnipeg or Vancouver, let us say, that there was no accommodation available for them. The result is that, so far as I am concerned, there has been a constant stream of correspondence from different parts of Canada with respect to this matter of the separated family allowance. I know the deputy ministers, who have just been under discussion, must have got pretty sick of my writing letters to them on this particular point. And while I have the opportunity I should like to pay tribute particularly to Mr. Sharpe, a man whom I have never met, but for whom I have high regard for the efficiency and patience he has displayed in trying to get around what was obviously a badly arranged regulation. I am wondering if the minister has got anywhere on this subject, because a month or so ago he did tell me that he would take a look at it.
The second point, in my judgment, is just as crazy. I have in mind the young man who enlists in the service at perhaps the age of 19 years and who, after enlisting, wants to get married. This is particularly so if the young man is going to be posted to Germany, but has a girl friend in Canada. He does not want to lose her, so he marries her before he leaves. After the marriage is arranged, apparently with the blessing of the service authorities, he finds that he cannot get the allowance for his wife because he is under the age of 21 years.


I think that is a silly regulation. It is obviously wrong. In the first place, if he is not entitled to the allowance he should not be given permission to marry. Secondly, if he is old enough to enter the service and go to Germany to stand guard over there, then I say he is entitled to the allowance granted a married person under the regulations.
While I am on my feet, and just so that I will not have to rise again, let me direct the minister's thoughts to another problem that I think is worthy of consideration. I refer to unemployment insurance as applied to service personnel. The regulations today are to the effect that, up to July of this year, anyone in the service is protected by way of unemployment insurance if he happens to decide to leave the service and take civil employment. However, anyone coming into the regular service after July of 1955 will not have unemployment insurance available to him.
In view of the fact that in my opinion the services are going to be permanent as long as most of us will live, they can be looked upon today as occupations for large numbers of young men who come in and enlist for periods of three or five years and intend to make it their calling. At the last sitting of the committee on veterans affairs a presentation was made by the Legion asking us to take a look at this problem. The law of averages will operate so that a considerable percentage of these young people will leave the services before their term has expired. Some of them will not be found suitable, or will not like it. When that happens members will be plagued with inquiries as to why they cannot get unemployment insurance, because members of the Korean division were given entitlement to it. These are the regulations today. The recommendation by the Legion was that service personnel after July 1955 should be considered in the same category as those employed in industry. In other words they were to be brought under the unemployment insurance provi: ions on a contributory basis, in exactly the same way as persons employed in industry.
The committee decided that a recommendation would be made to the Minister of National Defence, because it is the business of that department. Previously, under the regulations, it came under the Department of Veterans Affairs, and contributions were paid through that department. However, we recommended that the matter should be brought to the attention of the Department of National Defence, and that some kind of interdepartmental committee should be set up to study the matter and to ascertain from service personnel themselves whether they want

to be covered by unemployment insurance on a contributory basis, or otherwise.
I know the minister cannot say either yes or no at the present time, but I think he should indicate to the house that a study will be made of the subject. I would be glad to have his comments on the points I have raised.

The hon. member for Cape Breton South and I have discussed the matter of the separated family allowance which is payable to married personnel where the husband has been moved abroad or to some point in Canada sufficiently far away that the family are left behind, or for some reason cannot go with him. Then there is the situation where housing cannot be obtained at the point to which the husband has been sent. That is the field in which most of the difficulty arises.
The man who has been moved is supposed to assure himself, either through his own inquiries, or those of his commanding officer, that there is accommodation available for his family. In many cases there are not places readily available for the families, and the result is that some families do remain separated, such as the one to which the hon. member has referred. There does not seem to be any better way of handling the question of separated family allowances than the way which has been developed up to this time.
Then, turning to the married allowances: that of course is a matter of long-standing differences of opinion. The reason the limitation is still in force is that it is felt that when a young man has enlisted and is spending his first year in the army, he ought to give his full attention to it, particularly as he is likely to be moved two or three times to different schools. It is felt that until the young man becomes assimilated in his job it is better for him, in the end, and better for him as a soldier, that this limitation be continued.
With regard to the question of unemployment insurance, we are giving this matter consideration, in the light of the recommendations of the committee, and, on general grounds, there is something to be said for it. Unfortunately, up until now we have not been able to discover any particular desire on the part of the men themselves to participate in a contribution arrangement. We are still studying the matter and we will continue to do so.

I agree with the observations of the minister but with respect to the separated family allowance, it is a long jump from Nova Scotia to Chilliwack, British Columbia, particularly when a man has his own home. In one case I have in mind the
Supply-National Defence man had his own home and his wife and family were quite comfortable. It would be much better to pay separated family allowance and leave the wife and family where they are because usually that is where they want to stay. But in order to qualify for the additional allowance the woman I have in mind had to leave her home and take her children to British Columbia. When she arrived there she found there was no accommodation for her. The same thing applied in Winnipeg. The woman was obliged to take her two or three children to Winnipeg and live in one room in a hotel and pay terrific rates which certainly could not be met by the separated family allowance. The department should have at least some administrative latitude in dealing with a man in the circumstances I have described. If he were able to tell the deputy minister -I have not very much faith in the commanding officers because they have many other things to do; I have a lot of faith in the judgment of the deputy ministers on this particular matter-if he were able to write in and describe his circumstances and say that he has a home and that his family are happy, perhaps other arrangements could be made. Why shift a wife and family out to an area where there is no accommodation? When you have a soldier going out to a place where there is no accommodation for his family, and his family follows him, you are really demobilizing that fellow, so far as the service is concerned, if he has to go out and search for accommodation. Some latitude should be given so that the allowance could be paid under extenuating circumstances of that kind.
A boy under 21 who applies to his commanding officer for permission to get married should get the lecture that the minister just gave us on that particular point. If he received that lecture it might offset his desire to get married until he was 21.

He would get married
anyway.

No; they get permission from their unit commanding officer. When the boy gets permission to marry he has every right to receive the married allowance. Anyway, I hope the minister will take another look at it. I am glad the unemployment insurance end of it is being considered.
I should like to make one observation, Mr. Chairman. If the young man who wants to get married gets his commanding officer's consent, he can do so.
He gets the allowance?

Yes.

Supply-National Defence Mr. Gillis: Not in the couple of cases I have in mind.

I cannot deal with specific cases, but it is my understanding that consent may be given. In other words, he has to have the consent of the commanding officer before he marries if he is to get his marriage allowance.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to be permitted to make a suggestion to the minister. Since the salaries of civil servants and judges have been increased every four or five years, I would suggest that he consider increasing the $2,500 to the widow of a former minister of national defence. Fifteen years have now gone by and she has had no increase. I ask him to consider it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

No, Mr. Chairman. When the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich spoke on June 16 he drew attention to the item in the white paper dealing with permanent home stations for the regular units of the Canadian army. The relevant point in the white paper reads as follows:
For regular field units of the Canadian army, permanent home stations are being developed across Canada. This development is intended to give greater stability to servicemen and their dependents, for as units complete periods of overseas service they will return to a permanent home location.
The item goes on to list the places at which the home stations will be established. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich commended the department for making this long overdue arrangement, because some units have no home stations at the present time.
I do not find that the minister subsequently made any reference to that when he was giving his limited answers to suggestions coming from this side of the house. Will he now indicate to the committee what regular field units are to have their home stations at the various points that are listed in the white paper?

Perhaps while I am getting that information I might answer the question asked by the hon. member this morning regarding the annual charges levied by provinces for motor vehicle plates and the annual charges for chauffeurs' licences, and with reference to gasoline tax. So far as charges in respect of vehicle registration are concerned, the following rates apply in respect to annual plates for these vehicles: Saskatchewan, $1; Quebec, $2.50; New Brunswick,
$2; Prince Edward Island, $2; Alberta, $1; British Columbia, $2; Nova Scotia, $1; and Newfoundland, $2. In Ontario, free; Manitoba,
$1; Yukon, $1. With regard to drivers' licences, 

no driver's registration fee is required in any province except Quebec where we will pay for armed forces personnel driving national defence vehicles a personal fee of $2.50 each year. In the other provinces we have been able to have the military certificate accepted and no civil card is required.
As regards gasoline, which I think was the subject matter of the third question asked, gasoline purchased on contract by the Department of National Defence is tax free; but in all provinces where emergency purchases are made which are not under contract the prevailing tax is levied, the same as in respect of all other persons.
How long has a driver's licence fee been paid in Quebec?
Starting July 1 of this year.

It has not
been operative in the past; why is it being paid starting in July?
That is correct.

Why is it
being paid now? Has there been a change in policy? Has the government of Quebec asked for it?

This is the result of considerable negotiations that have gone on. The government of Quebec expressed to us some time ago the feeling that they were not willing to accept our evidence of identity of drivers, and the only way in which they could check under their own provincial regulation was to issue their own cards. We have agreed to that.
Would the minister care to comment on the constitutional aspect of it?

I am informed that these are not drivers' licences in the ordinary sense, they are certificates of identity and competency which we are supposed to see that each driver possesses. I understand they are registered in Quebec and to register these certificates which we provide the drivers as of July 1 there is to be a charge.

This seems to be a rather extraordinary situation where one province can come along and demand this kind of registration on the part of drivers of the Canadian army who drive in Quebec. I assume that if Quebec can levy this charge against the government the other provinces will have the same right.
That is so.
How many licences will be issued and what will it cost the government?

This comes into effect only tomorrow and I am sorry but we have not been able to make an estimate with any accuracy as to how many people will be involved.
I cannot give the hon. member even an approximate figure.

Is this not a dangerous precedent? Other provinces may come along and ask for the same licences and the same payments and so on. This may be extended to all government institutions. Is not this in fact a retreat from the position that has always been taken by the crown in the right of the dominion?

I understand that our legal officers who have discussed this with the province of Quebec and arrived at this formula take the view that the crown is not liable to tax by a province. Generally they uphold that view, but they feel that in this particular matter we are paying the province of Quebec for registration certificates and not paying a tax.

I certainly think that this
is a dangerous precedent and it should be looked into far more closely, not just by the law officers of the department but by the law officers of the crown. The whole government should be advised of this new position that has been taken. This may have most serious consequences in the future. It may be extended and this could be cited as a precedent. Other provinces could come along and demand certain payments and cite this as a precedent. I think before this is approved a careful investigation should be made by the government of its legal rights and there should be careful consultation with the law officers of the crown and if necessary a reference to the Supreme Court of Canada to decide just what are the rights of the dominion in matters of this kind.

As I mentioned when I was giving the figures, we have paid licence plate fees for many years. Each of the provinces provides us with plates for which we are charged, $2 in some cases and $1 in others as in the case of Saskatchewan. I presume if we followed the same line of argument adduced by my hon. friend we could say that that is also a tax. In the one case a licence plate is provided to be put on the car and in the other case a certificate of identity and fitness is provided which must be carried by our drivers when driving in Quebec. I do not know whether there is any substantial difference between the two cases. I would not hold myself out as a constitutional authority however.
Supply-National Defence Mr. Stewart (Winnipeg North): I think there is a difference and perhaps it should be referred to the department of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I should like to know if there have been complaints about the competency of service drivers from other provinces and, if so, have other provinces asked for the same certificates of fitness in relation to men in our armed services.
I do not think they have set up an external affairs department in Quebec but I believe it was suggested some time ago.
Have there been complaints from other provinces about the competency and fitness of army drivers?

No. May I reply to the hon.
member for Winnipeg South Centre who asked for the names of the regiments and the different home stations which we are constructing for them. The home stations and the regiments are as follows: Gagetown: Black Watch, an artillery regiment, an armoured regiment; Valcartier, Royal 22nd; London, Royal Canadian Regiment; Peta-wawa, the Canadian Guards; Winnipeg, an artillery regiment; Picton, an anti-aircraft regiment; Edmonton, P.P.C.L.I.; Calgary, the Queen's Own, an armoured regiment.

interest and local support have played in fashioning these units, out of which their noble service has sprung. I hope it is not too late to reverse a decision which, it seems to me, is bound to result in a very serious loss.

Mr. Chairman, the regular forces should be located at the most desirable locations. The Queen's Own Rifles (regular) have never been stationed in Toronto.
As far as the militia regiment is concerned I would not take exception to the eulogy of the Queen's Own by the hon. member. They are a fine regiment. As a matter of fact, it is on account of their record and their seniority-and the same thing applies to the Black Watch of Montreal-that these two regiments were selected to provide names for the two new regiments. It was never intended that permanent units would be identified permanently with any particular city. We have had no difficulty in Montreal with respect to the Black Watch regiment being stationed in the maritimes. We have had some complaint from a number of Toronto members with respect to the Queen's Own, but our senior officers have conferred with the complainants and explained the situation; I have not heard anything further about the matter since, until the hon. member made his remarks just now.
The militia battalion, of course, remains in Toronto. Any person wishing to join the Queen's Own, if he is enlisting in the regular army, can designate the Queen's Own and will be sent to the Queen's Own. I was told when I was last in Toronto that many men pass through the militia regiment to the regular regiment. I would hope that the people of Toronto who have for long been active supporters of the Queen's Own militia regiment will continue to give that support.
Apart from having a home station other than Toronto, it must be recognized that the Queen's Own battalions as regular units are apt to be sent to Korea or to Germany or to any other point. They are regular units, and are sent where necessity requires. In addition, the costs of establishing a home station in Toronto or adjacent to it are very high as compared with smaller cities. Also, in this particular case the Queen's Own will have another unit of the regular army service associated with it for training purposes, which is something to be desired.
I do not think the hon. member or the people of Toronto should feel dissatisfied or hurt at the fact that the Queen's Own regular regiment is being located in Calgary. I think they should be proud that their regiment has such a record that its name was selected as the name of a new regiment. I would hope

they would not only give it every support in the future, as they have in the past, but that it would become more closely affiliated with the militia regiment and that it would be reinforced more and more by the people of the Toronto area through that channel.

Mr. Chairman, I do not
propose to repeat what I said when speaking earlier. I should like to tell the minister, however, that I am aware of the discussions which have been carried on with him and his department on the part of those who represent the regiment. I would not wish him to think that he has satisfied those who have spoken to him on behalf of the regiment that his proposed location of the permanent home station of the Queen's Own Rifles of Canada in Calgary has met with their approval or that he has convinced them, as he has sought to do.
I should like to turn to one other matter of a different nature. I should like to ask the minister to say something to the committee as to the part the department has assigned to Maple Leaf Services, and the role that it intends that service to play with respect to men's army canteens. When he has done that, perhaps I should like to make some observations on the subject.

The Maple Leaf Services in the army has been incorporated, somewhat along the lines of NAAFI in Britain, to meet what we think is a need and to develop what we think will be a benefit to the men of the services. It is a corporate entity and a nonprofit organization. The benefits will accrue to army personnel. Up to the present time it has been within the jurisdiction of each commanding officer to look after the amenities on his station for the benefit of the men and their families, generally to make their living conditions much more pleasant.
This responsibility has grown to be a large and complicated matter because various commanding officers have different ideas, different problems, and different set-ups. The feeling has been that if this composite organization could be brought together under one merchandising head and staff, instituting standard practices throughout the units, the benefits which would accrue to the men would be greater in the aggregate. Second, it was felt that the profit which is made in the larger centres-some small portion of it at least- might be shared with other centres where there are now inadequate amenities.
The department, of course, is not involved in this. Maple Leaf Services is an organization which is for the benefit of army personnel. It has opened one store in Germany, as well as a club, and is now organizing to take
Supply-National Defence over facilities of the army in Canada. In taking this step I think it is following fairly well established practice such as that of NAAFI in Britain and PX in the United States. We think it is a forward step in the interests of the men themselves and of their families.

I was not quite clear as to the relationship of Maple Leaf Services to the department as such. The minister indicates that it is established as a separate corporate entity, as a non-profit making corporation without share capital. But what part does the department play in this corporation and in giving it its opportunity to take over what was formerly the prerogative of the local commands?

The corporation is run as any other corporation, by a board of directors who are senior officers of the army. There is one other factor in the organization of Maple Leaf Services Limited, or rather there are two other factors which might be mentioned. Accounting responsibilities in relation to the larger military units, responsibilities which rested on the C.O., became very heavy, and frequently he was not able to give these matters the careful attention one would want. Further the department was faced with a very complicated and difficult scheme of audit to keep conversant with the affairs of all these small units. It was felt that by having them organized into one organization and on one basis, better results could be obtained. The experience of other countries which we have studied led us to establish Maple Leaf Services here.
Am I to understand that the department does appoint the personnel of the corporation? It is really being operated by the department but in the convenient form of a non-profit making corporation?

The board is composed of the senior officers of the service. But the interrelation of regimental funds and departmental funds with the proceeds that come from these various activities will now be ended, and the picture will be clear by itself. It will be operated in that way and audited in that way. It will be an entity on its own although, as the hon. member says, as to final control, we have to keep our eye on it because after all it is dealing with all the personnel of the army.

I think I understand more clearly now. The department really controls Maple Leaf Services completely. It can appoint the personnel of the board of directors,
5514	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence and I suppose it can change those directors as it pleases. Am I correct in that assumption?
The composition of the board of directors is provided in the incorporation papers and they are senior army officers.
But it is the department which will decide who are the future directors from time to time?

I am speaking now from memory, but I think the positions of the officers who will be the directors are set out in the incorporation papers. From time to time different senior officers will succeed each other so there is continuity. But the army senior officers will have the responsibility of seeing that the scheme is operated properly. There is no question about that.

Am I correct in my understanding that this is confined to the operation of the men's canteen in the army only, that it does not extend to the Royal Canadian Air Force or to the Royal Canadian Navy, and that it does not extend either to officers or sergeants in the army?

As of the present, Maple Leaf Services applies only to the army. It has no jurisdiction with regard to the other two services. It does not take in sergeants' messes or officers' messes. Its function is to look after merchandising, amenities such as bowling alleys and theatres and all the men's own perquisites which they develop either with the assistance of the department or on their own behalf.
Who will establish the salaries of the senior officials? Will they be subject to approval by the department?

No. The board of directors has authority to fix the salaries and to engage the necessary civilians, because these operations are largely staffed by civilians and will be run as any other commercial enterprise.
But will the department have no concern about the salaries that are set by the board of directors of the corporation?

I do not think there is any direct responsibility. Of course we will from time to time-and that is one of the prime requisites of this set-up-have the benefit of complete audits and statements, something we have never been able to get before. I would expect that the directors of the corporation would be aware of any salaries paid which were out of line, or any charges that were made that were exorbitant, or any irregularities which might occur. But we are 

modelling this on a type of organization which has succeeded very well elsewhere. It is an experiment in our case, identified as yet only with the army.
Do I take it, for instance, that the minister and his officials do not know what are the salaries that have been established by Maple Leaf Services for its senior officials?
No, we do not necessarily know except as we have reports. We did appoint three officers at certain salaries to start the organization.
Could the minister give us the salaries of those he knows?

What was done was to call out three officers to set up the organization. They are still on strength on a call-out basis, and as soon as the corporation is functioning properly they will become officers of the corporation. This was a temporary step which was taken just to get the corporation started.
Can the minister give us the salaries he knows? He said he knew several.

I do not have the figures of the salaries, but probably my hon. friend would be satisfied if I were to tell him that the senior official is a brigadier and that there are two lieutenant colonels who have been called out. If the hon. member will look at page 35 of the white paper I think he can find the information without too much difficulty.
I take it these officers, who are really on loan to Maple Leaf Services, are to be paid by Maple Leaf Services at their regular army rates of pay according to their rank. Is that the arrangement now?

Their call-out will cease as soon as the organization is completed, and their civilian salaries will not necessarily have any relation to their present call-out pay and allowances. Their salaries will be dealt with along with all other salaries. The idea is that it will be a civilian organization operated by civilians for the benefit of the men in the army. All the steps we have taken up to now have been purely temporary steps to get the corporation organized and working.

Then I take it from the minister's answer that on this temporary basis there are certain officers really on loan from the department to the corporation and that they are continuing to draw rates of pay according to their rank and that pay is being charged against the corporation. After the temporary period is ended salaries will be established by the corporation for these

officers and for employees, but that has not been done yet and the minister does not know what these salaries will be. Have I stated that correctly?

I think the statements of the hon. member are correct, with the exception that I should like to make it clear that until some cut-off date, which has not yet been established, the salaries of the three officers to whom I have referred will be paid by the army. After that they will go on the civilian strength of the corporation.

I hope the minister will be patient. I have several more questions, because this is an interesting innovation, I believe, as far as the Canadian army is concerned. First of all, what is going to be the relationship between the local commanding officer and the operation of the canteen, no longer under the local command but under an arrangement under which that local canteen will be responsible to Maple Leaf Services?

I understand that the local managers of these institutions will be civilians. Many of them will be local civilians. I think many of them are already in the institutions. So far as policy is concerned, general direction will come from Ottawa, from the directors of the corporation or the general manager who will in turn co-operate, of course, as they do in NAAFI, with the local military commanders who are naturally interested. But as a commercial organization, and to the extent that these institutions are commercial institutions, their policy will be laid down by the management of Maple Leaf Services.
I do not think it is anticipated that there will be any particular difficulty. As far as I know, there has not been any particular difficulty in connection with NAAFI or PX, but there must be co-operation between the army and the civilian management of the corporation. It seems to have worked out well in practice elsewhere, and we hope it will work out well here.

The minister indicated that there will now be an opportunity for an audit, and that this being a non-profit making corporation the profits would be used, as I understood him to say some few minutes ago, for the benefit of the men. Will he enlarge on that and indicate how the profits are to be used? Are they to be used for local benefit or how are they to be distributed if not on the local basis?

The percentages have not been worked out, because they are related to the size of the operation, but I understand
Supply-National Defence the disposition of the profits will be twofold. First of all, part of the profits will go to the regimental funds, and part will go to the army welfare fund which it is intended to set up along the lines of the navy benevolent fund or the air force benevolent fund. The net profits of the corporation will be divided between these two objects in a proportion yet to be established.
Are we to understand there is no idea yet as to the relative size of the two parts into which the profits are to be divided?

No. The corporation is just beginning to get organized in Canada. Such organization work as has been done up to now has been done only where it was felt to be more needed, in Germany. The organization stage here is just being initiated. There will have to be a good deal of study and assessment made, and I think there is going to be a disposition not to be quite as generous with the very profitable organizations as formerly and a little more generous with other units. Some sort of reasonable adjustment will be made in the case of units where these things are needed just as badly but where the turnover or volume is not as great. The idea is to provide from the profits of all the units, where needed and to the extent needed, the best possible division of amenities and assistance for the benefit of the men.

I hope the minister will not mind if I ask another question or two. I have some interest in the subject. I had the unpleasant duty at one time of having to supervise the operation of one of these canteens, and I can appreciate some of the problems involved.
What is going to be the buying policy, or has a buying policy been arrived at? The minister is aware, of course, that when the canteens were on a local basis under local command and local operation the buying was done through local jobbers. Is that going to continue to be the policy, or does the department contemplate that Maple Leaf Services will ignore the local jobber and attempt to deal with the manufacturer? Will it do its purchasing on a strictly national basis, without regard to any local supplier or jobber?

I would say that the policy will be to do both. There are certain commodities that can be purchased much more economically in quantity, and many are of local origin. I think the intention will be to utilize both methods of purchase, in the light of cost and convenience. There is no intention to by-pass the normal channels of commercial activity or to cut unduly the prices
5516	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence at which other people are selling commodities. Nor is there any intention of centralizing all the buying at headquarters or of doing all the buying locally. Those are things which I think will fall into place when the studies are completed; and as the corporation takes over areas. I should think those things will adjust themselves reasonably well.

I am glad to hear the minister indicate that he has some appreciation of the importance of not letting everything be centralized, because it strikes me that in connection with an innovation like this there are some very serious dangers connected with the possibility of the centralization of buying. I believe that centralization could have some very unhappy results, and one of those results could be a very dull uniformity and a lack of imagination in connection with local canteens and the commodities on sale there.
There is also the factor of service to be considered. By and large these local canteens have depended very substantially on local jobbers for service. I do not think that in a case of mass buying, or centralized buying, the factor of service could be expected to be as it would be if a serious attempt were made to use the services of the local suppliers and jobbers. I take it we may have the assurance of the minister that due regard will be had in the purchasing policy for the undoubted services that can be rendered by local jobbers and suppliers in respect of the very wide variety of commodities of all kinds that are on sale at these canteens.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall we proceed to the next item?
I think the minister would wish to make some comment.

I am sure that when this corporation gets under way a good deal of responsibility in each case will rest on the local manager. And I would feel sure, too, that he, working with the community, and knowing the people from whom he might acquire the goods for his whole operation, would want to be a part of the community.
As I said some time ago, the way to be part of a community is to trade within it. However, I do not think I would want to undertake that there would be a hard and fast rule that all purchasing would be local, or a hard and fast rule that all purchasing would be done centrally, because I do not think either would be exactly right. I think there would be a combination of the two. In the last analysis I have no doubt a good deal will depend upon the good will of the local manager, because after all this involves


a large assortment of local commercial institutions, moving picture houses and the like, throughout Canada.
I think the central organization in Ottawa will be more concerned about keeping track of the funds, auditing those funds and seeing that everything is in order, something which has been very difficult of achievement in the past, as I think the hon. member knows. I do not believe there will be any disposition to upset a domestic market or to get into any local price wars. There is no intention of anything of that kind.

There is one further aspect of the matter on which I seek information. What Maple Leaf Services is in process of doing is the taking over of these canteens from existing establishments. What arrangements are being made in connection with the taking over? Undoubtedly there are stocks and inventories on hand as well as premises. What is being done about taking over; and in particular, what has been done with the profits accruing recently on the operation of the canteens, and in the course of the sale of their remaining inventories to Maple Leaf Services?

The procedure is that each locality is being studied and checked, and will be taken over when all the information that should be known is known. I would presume that each case will be adjusted on its merits. This is just beginning to be done now, so I cannot give an example. The idea is to deal with these local situations gradually, as fast as possible, and bring them into the main company.

Then will the minister deal with the latter part of my question. I was talking about the profits accruing latterly in this period from the operations, and profits presumably that may accrue on the turning over of the inventory by the local units to Maple Leaf Services. Who will own them?

I speak subject to correction, but my understanding^ is that in any given local situation the first thing that will be done is to fix a cut-off date. Then they will make their adjustment as of that date as between the old dispensation and the new. I believe I am correct in saying that up to a certain point they will follow the old method of distribution or the old method of disposing of profits. After the cut-off date, whatever method is evolved by Maple Leaf Services would be followed from then on.

Mr. Chairman, to use a military term, I would like to break step in this rather serious discussion of national

defence matters and would speak for a few moments on a matter which most-
If the hon. member does not mind, and if he is going to turn to another subject, there are other hon. members who wish to develop further the subject now under discussion.

The minister has intimated that at least some of the purchasing will be done from a central point in connection with the supplying of stores to canteens. Does this mean that it is planned to operate a central warehouse? If so, from what point will goods be distributed; or will it be a case of purchasing for several units and then making individual shipments to the various units concerned?

As I have already pointed out, the practical side of this operation is just now beginning to get under way. Except in a general way I have no knowledge of the exact procedure the directors of the corporation will follow. I should think they would follow the procedure of any corporation engaged in this kind of business; that they would study the local needs in the areas concerned, and would decide whether they should have a warehouse at a certain point, or whether the business there was sufficiently small that it could be served from somewhere else. There is a great deal of work to be done on this yet. We have not really got fully under way. I would think the management of Maple Leaf Services will be in duty bound to study those problems. They are going to try to operate in an efficient and satisfactory way for the benefit of the people whom they are serving. The questions the hon. member has asked I am sure will be very much in their minds. I do not think they have resolved them yet.

I should like to point
out, Mr. Chairman, that it has been found, particularly in food distribution, that the established jobbers are in a position to handle merchandise much more efficiently and at a lower cost than even some of the largest chain organizations; so much so, in fact, that some chain organizations have themselves utilized the services of those jobbers. I just leave that thought with the minister and with the members of his staff who are interested in this.

I have a question along the same line as the last series of questions. I assume that Maple Leaf Services are going to take over the work that was formerly done by what was known as the volunteer services. I wonder whether this new system results from the fact that any 50433-348
Supply-National Defence of those four which were active during or since the last war has asked to be relieved of its responsibilities in so far as providing amenities to the troops is concerned.

No, I do not think there has been any formal application from these organizations or from any of them to be relieved of this work; but it has been felt that as Maple Leaf Services primarily will be handling a peacetime situation within Canada in the main, the method that has been used in other countries would appear to be the most effective and the best to adopt.
So far as Germany is concerned-I think I am right in this; it was before my time-I believe the only suggestion that came from any of the organizations in the first place, and this is evidently what is in the mind of my hon. friend, was that the Salvation Army asked to be permitted to set up at Soest. That was given. They are still there. I recollect no other application, but I do not think with the situation as it is now in Canada, with home stations and with regular forces of substantial size, the question really will arise. I think the accepted way, which as I have said, has operated in other countries, is that we ought to be sure these things are provided; we ought to see that they are operated properly; we ought to see that their returns are audited properly and that the men receive the benefits from their operations.
The minister is not suggesting that all these things were not done by the voluntary organizations which formerly provided the services?

No, I am not suggesting that at all. All I am saying is that it is now a peacetime proposition all over Canada, and its magnitude will be very substantial. I certainly would not reflect on the operations of any of these other groups during the time they were operating. If I implied that, it was entirely involuntary, because I had no such thought in mind.

Even if this service is carried on all over Canada, surely it will not be nearly of the magnitude of the service that was carried on during the last war by the four voluntary organizations, the Salvation Army, the Knights of Columbus, the Canadian Legion and the Y.M.C.A. What I should like to know is, were these people consulted on providing this service as was done before, or was this a unilateral action taken by the members of the general staff?

It is one thing to have this service provided in a time of war when

Supply-National Defence everybody is volunteering to do the thing they can do best and to give the best service. There is a spirit of sacrifice and of interest that is very deep and very moving. The situation that we now have in Canada in the army is that we are going to have, presumably for quite some time, a reasonably large permanent force, and we feel the method we have adopted will serve the purpose continually over a period of years, but not on a voluntary agency basis.
The other factor entering into the matter is this. The institutions which did so well during the war had to be subsidized very largely by the federal government. We hope that Maple Leaf Services will not have to be subsidized, but that it will return in the aggregate adequate profits to perform what it is supposed to do without any assistance from the taxpayers.

Of course that results from the fact that most of the things that were provided through those services were given free of charge; whereas I assume that now the personnel in the services are going to have to pay for anything they receive. Will the minister tell us whether a start was made on this type of organization during the Korean campaign?
No, this has followed the Korean campaign.
Do I understand that in the event of actual hostilities there is no definite plan to forgo the type of organization we had in the previous war?
No; no consideration has been given to that.

How does this type of organization work right down to the unit level that we are talking about, such as manoeuvres in Germany, at Gagetown or at other such places? How do the amenities under this plan the minister has in mind get down to the ordinary man who is carrying the rifle in the field, or in exercises that may take place here and in Germany?
I am not sure that I understand the hon. member. Is he referring to amenities such as tea wagons and things that go around to the troops?

As I recall it, Mr. Chairman, they were operating an assortment of many things that filtered down to the battle level of the forces. Whether it was tooth brushes, tooth paste or something else, it seemed to get through. What I am trying to get at is this. Is there to be a responsible army officer in the unit who will see that this Maple Leaf source of supply will get down to the level of the infantry soldier, or is it
[Mr. CampneyJ

going to stop somewhere along the line in the canteen, and if you can get it, fine; otherwise you do not get it? That is a very simple question.

Generally speaking, as I said some time ago, it will be provided in the canteen. The expectation is that there will be close collaboration between the army officers interested in these things, or who have some responsibility for their men, and the commercial organization which will have on its directorate senior officers in the army. It is felt that this relationship will characterize the two branches and that, as in other countries, they will work harmoniously together in the common interests of one group of people, namely the men in the army and their families.

I do not want to carry this on with any feeling of animosity, but the question of whether the general manager of Maple Leaf Services gets along with the chief of the general staff is not going to help the man in the field in providing him with amenities. Should there not be a properly designated officer at the company or regimental level whose responsibility it would be to see that the things made available through this organization get to the men in the field?

Officers must be responsible for the welfare of their men, as they always have been. This is not intended to supplant any proper interest that an officer should have in his men. It is hoped that this will make more amenities available, and perhaps an officer will not have the same difficulty in looking after his men. There is no intention of carrying this matter to the point where it becomes a predominant factor in operating the army.

I would suggest to the minister that that is not an answer to my question. I am not going to pursue the matter, except to say that if that is the type of organization that is intended, then the ordinary infantryman carrying a rifle and the ordinary tankman in a tank is not going to get the same amenities that he would have received from the organization we once had. Even if they are available at the level suggested by the minister they must seep down to the men in the field. If this is the system that is to be set up I suggest, quite apart from the responsibility of the unit officer for the welfare of his troops, that someone should be designated whose responsibility it would be to guarantee that these amenities are made available at the levels at which they should be available.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to break step, using a military term, for a few minutes in this serious discussion on national defence. I should like to deal briefly with a matter which some hon. members may consider trivial; but we should not forget that if we look after the small things, the large ones will take care of themselves.
You can purchase the best in arms, the best in tanks, naval vessels and aeroplanes, but the best weapon of all is the good morale of our personnel. There can be no argument against the need for cultural and social activities in the armed forces. There is much spare time in the barracks and camps and outposts and time hangs heavy for lonely men. Considerable funds have been expended in providing brass bands, bugle bands and pipe bands. They are all good and are providing a wonderful service to our army. They are a credit to the army.
Many of us have served in the army, and we know the lift that was given to our spirits when someone started a good marching song. I think it is high time the Canadian army learned to sing. I say that seriously. I mean it is time they learned to sing in parts; first and second bass, and first and second tenor, and when you have the ladies with you, soprano and alto. Of course the best lift of all is given by a military band. It is a real chin-lifter which relieves the monotony and boredom and fatigue which may face our men. I think there are times in this house when a good song would be most ^useful.
Brass bands cost money, and they are not always available. Bugle bands are excellent, but they are not always available. No investment is needed to have men sing together, and no transport is required to carry the equipment. Men stationed in distant radar stations and other outposts could participate with nothing more than a little training. We all remember the popular marching songs such as "Tipperary", "Mademoiselle from Armen-tieres" and many others. But we just shouted those songs, we did not sing them. We simply shouted at the top of our voices and there was no thought of harmony. However, they were great chin-lifters. I know we would be surprised at the satisfaction and benefit that would ensue if these men were given some training so they could sing in parts.
Between the wars I made several visits to Europe, and I attended the Olympic games in Berlin in 1936. When there I heard German boy scouts, workers, servicemen and others marching and singing, and it was really wonderful. I could not understand the words but you could see its effect and how it relieved fatigue. This cannot be denied.
50433-348J
Supply-National Defence Canadian soldiers could be trained to sing in harmony. All that is required is an organized effort to train our service personnel in male or mixed choir singing, singing in parts. Under proper direction this cultural activity would be of great value for recreational purposes and the building up of morale, and could be done at very little expense. Competitions in choral singing could be promoted among units in the armed forces. I am sure this would prove beneficial in times of stress and strain. I should like to see this developed to the extent where Canada's army would be known as Canada's singing army.

Mr. Chairman, as the hon. member for Waterloo North has suggested, we should break step. I agree that we should, but I am suggesting that we should re-group and re-form. I should like to draw the attention of the minister and the committee to a problem with which we are faced in our part of the country. I have noticed that our friends on the opposition benches have been talking in dollars and cents. Dollars and' cents are one of the important things with which we have to deal. However, the morale-of our fighting men is not gauged at all times; by dollars and cents.
At this time I should like to bring to the attention of the minister the famous North Nova Scotia Highlanders. The North Nova Scotia Highlanders were not talking dollars and cents when they landed on the Normandy beaches on D-day. Under the new concept of organization of the so-called reserve army or militia, this famous regiment is to be in the land of the forgotten. There are many young Nova Scotians who have a fondness for the traditions of this great regiment.
Once again I urge the minister, as I have before on the floor of this house, to see that m his reorganization of the militia the name of the North Nova Scotia Highlanders is carried forward and not just absorbed into the name of the Nova Scotia Highlanders, first battalion (north). If he will do that he will be doing one of the greatest things that can be done to keep alive the traditions of this force of fighting men who have carried their weight in every war in which Canada has participated.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to support the remarks made by the hon member for York West as well as the observations made by the hon. member for Waterloo North. I think they are closely related, notwithstanding the fact that he suggested we were breaking step in the discussion.
I have been interested in this matter of welfare for the troops ever since I came

Supply-National Defence into the house in 1951. I agree with the minister to a certain extent, that in a continuing peacetime army an organization of the nature he has outlined here this afternoon is required. However, in connection with Canadian army personnel serving abroad a slightly different difficulty enters the picture. It has been pointed out from time to time that, particularly for single men in the armed forces, the social situation in which they find themselves is extremely difficult. They lack all the amenities of home and, as a result, from time to time we hear reports of behaviour problems amongst our men serving abroad.
I believe the minister compared the Maple Leaf Services arrangement with the NAAFI arrangement that was quite common in the United Kingdom forces during the war. Some of the Canadian personnel serving abroad, particularly those who served on R.A.F. stations, came into touch with NAAFI. It was a civilian organization designed to meet welfare and service problems. I found that NAAFI did a good job so far as providing tea and buns and that kind of service was concerned. However, I also discovered that it lacked the personal relations touch that was peculiar to the voluntary organizations that served the Canadian armed forces in such an outstanding way during world war I and world war II.
I believe the Canadian serviceman abroad needs more than tea and buns, chocolate bars, cigarettes and so forth. Those are essential, of course; but there is also the more elusive service that can be provided where the personnel providing those services have special qualities of heart and mind that help to bring the serviceman who is away from his native country more closely in touch with home. Therefore I would suggest very strongly that, in circumstances where Canadian forces are required to serve outside their shores, very careful consideration be given to the representations of the voluntary organizations.
In reply to a question by the hon. member for York West, I believe, the minister indicated that only one such voluntary organization made any such representation. I think he will recall that at the time of the Korean crisis all voluntary organizations were very active in their representations, and unfortunately their services were not made use of at the time. I should also like to suggest that, in the case of the organization already serving Canadian forces in Germany, every available opportunity be given to allow them to provide this extra kind of service right down to the unit level.
= There is one further question I should like to ask on this subject. I am wondering

whether the canteens that are being provided through Maple Leaf Services facilities are wet or dry canteens; that is, whether there are separate wet and dry canteens or whether those facilities are combined. I think that concludes the representations I wish to make on this subject.
Dry canteens and wet canteens are, of course, separate, though both will be operated by Maple Leaf Services. They will not be combined.

I should like to ask just one further question. In reference to voluntary organizations serving in what might be called peacetime theatres of operation in these cold war days, are any facilities provided to such organizations in the way of free conveyance in military transports and so forth, in order to bring their amenities to the field of operation?

As the hon. member probably knows, our transport to Germany is civilian. It is paid for by the Department of National Defence, the same as in respect of other people who travel. There is no free transport provided as far as the brigade is concerned.

Mr. Chairman, I am rising at this time because of a statement the minister made a while ago in answer to a question by my hon. friend from Winnipeg South Centre, in which he asked about the location of the various regiments in Canada. The minister stated that the Black Watch will be stationed in New Brunswick. I read in the press a while ago that one of those undisclosed and unknown prominent spokesmen in the Department of National Defence had said that the Black Watch might be moved, or probably would be moved, to Gagetown some time in the future, but after that the minister rapped all these unknown spokesmen across the knuckles.
I was hoping that those spokesmen had been wrong and had been disqualified, and I was waiting to hear my hon. friend say something about it. One battalion of the Black Watch is stationed at Aldershot, in my constituency, and it has been there for some considerable time. It was hoped and believed, until this unknown spokesman issued his ukase, that that battalion would remain there. I realize, of course, that this move is not going to take place now but at some considerable time in the future. I know the minister with his broadminded attitude and his deliberate judgment can resurvey the situation and perhaps change his mind and make sure that the Black Watch does stay in Aldershot.

The camp at Aldershot, which has been there for generations, maintains the name and the traditions of the old camp in Britain, with which the British army and the Canadian army have been so closely associated. It is something that is worth preserving. It would be unfortunate if that camp were left to be occupied by a few members of the reserve army in summertime or by boy scouts or girl guides or whoever it might be. The department has spent a good deal of money in rehabilitating that camp. I have been told by some officers who occupied responsible positions in the department that in case of emergency-and I use that euphemistic phrase not too loosely-there would be a definite place for Aldershot. If at some future time it is necessary to send troops across the seas, in the event that a war should come, Aldershot is essential as an embarkation point, a place that would have to be used in connection with the dispatch of troops through the ports of eastern Canada. Therefore I believe the camp should be maintained.
It would also be a good thing for the men to have it maintained. They could be located at no better place in Canada. I realize they have to go to Gagetown for summer training from time to time, but surely it is not necessary to have all the troops centred at Gage-town.
We have had a discussion in the last few minutes on morale and the general safeguarding of the interests of the personnel. We need training in motor transport. It is relatively a few miles, a nice day's trip, to move men by motor from Aldershot to Gage-town. Therefore, from the standpoint of the welfare of the men as well as from the standpoint of the department I hope the minister did not mean to be quite as direct as he was this afternoon. If he did, then he had some other unit in mind which will be coming into that camp.
So much for that. Somebody has said that we are getting out of step. We are not only out of step here but we have beaten the gun. The hon. member for Colchester-Hants was speaking a few moments ago not on this item but on the next one, the matter of the reserve army. I have something to say on that subject, and I hope the minister will reserve any comments he has on that matter until we come to the reserve army.

I want to direct the attention of the minister to another problem. I refer now to the paragraph on page 22 of the white paper headed "Women in the Services". I think it is well worth while considering this matter. The paragraph reads:
As at December 31, 1954, there were 6,600 women in the regular and reserve forces of the three

services. Of the 3,346 women in the regular forces 64 were in navy, 203 in army, and 3,076 in air force. Of the 3,314 women in the reserve forces 928 were in navy, 1,558 in army, and 828 in air force. The R.C.A.F. continues to recruit women for the regular force for clerical, stenographic, radar, telecommunications and other duties. Except for nursing and other allied services and a few key personnel, the army continues to recruit women for the reserve force only.
I suggest to the minister that the department should reconsider its position with regard to the employment of women in the services. It is not right that in the one service, the regular air force, women should be employed to the extent of 3,076, and in the regular army only to the extent of 203. Women could be employed in the regular army for duties similar to those for which they are employed in the R.C.A.F. It is not necessary to dwell upon the useful services of women in both wars, particularly in the second world war. They fulfilled all the tasks allotted to them in the services with distinction. They are very competent, very conscientious and most reliable. There is no question but that they could be employed now in the peacetime organization of the regular army, just as the air force employs them.
I am well aware there are many women now serving in the reserve force who would welcome the opportunity of employment with the regular army. The employment of perhaps 3,000 to 5,000 women in the regular army would at the same time assist the army in its organization and help it to reach the -quota that has been set for it. Women would also, quite naturally, occupy clerical positions and do things of that nature which they can really perform better than men, and would thus release men for more active employment in the field.
I think we are making a mistake in not enlisting more women in the army. If the air force can do it, why cannot the army do it? What are the objections? We have been all through this in two wars. The experiment entered upon so timidly in the first war was accepted as a proper procedure in the second and was carried on very successfully. Recently in the reserve force I happened to have command of a manning depot for a three-year period, and these manning depots enlist quite a number of women.
Now that I am no longer connected with the militia I do not feel restrained in commenting upon anything with regard to that branch of the service. My experience with women in the manning depot, as well as from having observed some of their work during the course of the second world war, is that it is all to the advantage of the country to use these people who are just as willing to serve
Supply-National Defence as men, and who can perform just as useful a service as men in certain branches of the service.
It is a mistake to employ able-bodied men for clerical work and other types of activity within the army when that same work can be done just as well, and often more efficiently, by women. They perhaps take to service work better than some men do, and are often more dependable and more interested in their work. They seem better fitted on occasion to do some of the tedious tasks that men find frustrating. The general experience of Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States is that women in the services are filling a Very useful purpose and should be so employed.
I should like the minister to inform the committee whether or not the policy of the department will tend toward the employment of more women in the services, and particularly in the regular army.

As the hon. member has said, the air force is more actively engaged in the recruiting of females into the service. It has of course a wider range of positions and activities in peacetime where the services of women can be utilized. It has been, as it were, leading in this particular tendency.
I think it is fair to say that the experience has not been wholly satisfactory, because the losses from the service through marriage and people who have left the service have been higher than we had anticipated. The air force is now assessing the success of its recruiting policy with respect to women. While that is being done, and until it is completed, no serious thought has been given, as the hon. member has suggested might be done, to recruiting women generally and in greater numbers in the other two services.

Would the minister say that the losses due to marriage and for other reasons exceed the losses in manpower the army has suffered from the desertions referred to a moment ago by the hon. member for Queens?

I understand that in the case of women in the air force the wastage is about 45 per cent. I do not know what the ratio of desertions and absentees is in the army, but it is a good deal lower than that.

When the minister was speaking on June 16, referring to planned expenditures for army equipment amounting to approximately $100 million, he said-
-including tooling lor production in Canada of the FN rifle for which standardized drawings have already been prepared.
Last year I had occasion to draw the attention of the then minister to the FN rifle, and we had a rather pleasant exchange of opinions across the floor. What is the situation now? To what extent do we propose to produce the rifle, and what countries have adopted it as the standard arm? Last year it was pointed out that trials were still under way to ascertain whether or not it could be used in northern areas and under very cold conditions. I presume those trials have proved satisfactory. Would the minister enlighten the committee now with regard to the FN rifle? What is the present stage of development, and what are the commitments for the future?

So far as Canada is concerned I might just mention that the expression I used, to which the hon. member referred, when I said that during the present year we planned expenditures for army equipment of approximately $100 million, including tooling for production in Canada of the FN rifle, has been interpreted as meaning that tooling for the FN rifle was to cost $100 million. I should point out that the tooling for the FN rifle was just mentioned incidentally in connection with the general equipment figure.
As to the production of the rifle, detailed plans translated into our system have been completed, and the Department of National Defence has placed with the Department of Defence Production an order for, I believe, 72,000 of these rifles. I understand tooling will commence immediately, and we will begin to receive them as fast as they can be produced. I have no dates in mind, but I think the details are pretty well settled.

With regard to the other question, as to what nations have adopted the FN rifle, of course Belgium-naturally, because it was originated there-and also the United Kingdom, as well as ourselves have adopted it.
Is our production of FN rifles based solely on providing our own forces with it, or have we orders from other countries for the rifle.
So far production is based entirely upon our own requirements. We have no orders in Canada for the provision of these rifles to any other country.
I note in the details an item for the construction of buildings and works in the amount of $67,500,000. How much of that is for British Columbia, and where will it be spent?
