Before we close off this section I should like to refer to another matter, Mr. Chairman. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre raised some serious questions dealing with the over-all army command in connection with its use of armour and its relation to the other arms of the army. As a matter of fact his remarks were also pointed up by the remarks of the hon. member for Greenwood. I do believe we are entitled to expect from the minister some answer to the criticism of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. If there is anyone in this house who is qualified to speak in connection with the over-all army picture and the use of armour it is that hon. member. He has been very strong in his condemnation of the over-all picture, and we should hear from the minister before we close off this section.

I do not wish to engage in a theoretical discussion about the merits of the different services, or the extent to which one should be developed, say, at the expense of the other. The establishments of our services, including armour, change. We try to keep in touch with late information, and we are watching the studies that are being made at NATO, in Great Britain and in the United States as to the relative strength of the different elements of the forces.
. Until now nothing has been static. There is no finality in these things. But when one is changing an establishment and changing a set-up, one must do a good deal of study because you do not do these things precipitously. Such changes usually come gradually. Until the present time the establishment of our forces reflects the very best thinking in our services and the most advanced thinking of our contemporaries abroad.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, to whom the hon. member for York West referred, disagrees with the judgment of the military advisers who advise me, and I do not know that any good purpose would be served by continuing a theoretical discussion at this moment. In the army we are endeavouring to produce the most effective, up to date and modern type of fighting man we can, in the light of our own experience and the experience of other countries. As I say, nothing is static. These things are always under review, but up to the moment the present establishment reflects our best thinking.

Can the minister answer the question that was raised? Is there any high-ranking officer in a position with

Supply-National Defence the over-all command of the army or connected with training who does come from the armoured corps?
If I recollect correctly the deputy chief of the general staff comes from the armoured corps.

I do not want to get into this again, but I am not sure that I was pleased with the suggestion of the minister that this is a theoretical matter. I think it is an entirely practical matter. The development of an efficient army is dependent upon experience of the past. Certainly a little theory has entered into it at some stage, if you are going beyond the experience of the past; but to term this a theoretical matter, or as something beyond the competence of this house, is to say something that has no practical effect.
. 1 think it is a wrong approach to the subject. There is nothing at all theoretical about suggestions that have been made from this side of the house with regard to the better employment of armour in the Canadian army. The whole purpose is to develop not only an efficient fighting force but, as I pointed out before, to provide adequate protection for the men who do the fighting.
I have adduced evidence from the records of the last war to show that tanks saved lives. That was the experience of the Germans. _ If you read the book published by Guderian, who was one of the most skilled tank commanders, you will discover that. If you will read the material published by our official historian, Colonel Stacey, you will discover that armoured troops suffered fewer casualties than did the infantry, yet achieved the objectives desired. Far from being theoretical, this is an intensely practical subject. I hope the minister will not dismiss it as just a theoretical discussion on the floor of the House of Commons, but will give it his earnest attention.
I grant that it may come into the realm of conflict with his advisers. That may well be; but the function of the Minister of National Defence is to assess problems of this nature and make decisions. He has only to review the development and use of armour by the armies of the world to discover the conflict with the high command that went on for years with regard to whether armour was effective on the battle field. There was the greatest division of opinion in between the two wars and that applied here in Canada, to the extent that we were operating cavalry regiments in the thirties when we should have been training light tank regiments.
IMr. Hamilton (York West).]

The cavalry disappeared on August 8 and 9, 1918, in France when cavalry horses were mowed down by machine gun fire. I walked over the battlefield and saw dead horses lying there in hundreds. Once the machine gun dominated the battlefield, as it did in the first great war, the doom of the horse cavalry was evident. But it took the military mind another 20 years to realize that fact.
What I am afraid of is that here in Canada we are neglecting to give full consideration to the lessons learned in the second world war in regard to the use of the armoured fighting vehicle on the battlefield and the practical saving of lives which is involved. I would not refer to the use of the armoured personnel carrier if it were not for the fact that it is the best known means at the present time of saving the lives of infantrymen. The armoured personnel carrier was operated by the Canadian armoured corps.
The function of the Minister of National Defence is not only to develop an effective fighting machine, but to do it in such a way that the lives of men are spared. That can be done by the proper use of armour under conditions of warfare such as we have known in our time. That is why I say it is not theoretical; it is practical, and my only hope is that before my time is concluded as a member of this house I shall have impressed upon the present minister of defence and those who hold high office in the defence department that more attention should be given to the use of armour.
I shall continue to deplore having infantry advance across open ground. As I said earlier today, I am sure that will be the exercise at Gagetown in a few weeks. It was slaughter in the first war, as anyone who survived that war knows. It was slaughter in the second great war. We lost thousands of Canadian soldiers in 1915, 1916, 1917 and 1918 because they had to move across open ground and through wheat fields on their own flat feet. We lost thousands of infantry soldiers in the second world war who had to do the same thing. Most infantry casualties after the landing on the Normandy beaches and in the subsequent fighting up to the battle of Falaise were due to the same causes that produced infantry casualties in the first great war, machine gun and mortar fire, against which the human body has no protection whatsoever.
Give these infantrymen the protection of armour, either by the use of the armoured personnel carrier or by using them as armoured corps troops in tanks, and you will save lives. What is so theoretical about that?' It is highly practical, and it should concern the Minister of National Defence and his

advisers. If his advisers do not understand this problem or do not see it-and I cannot for the life of me apprehend why they cannot see it-then it is up to the Minister of National Defence to determine for himself, to examine the record.
There is no use talking to men who hold high command and are not familiar with the use of armour. How can such men possibly know the situation. If such a man has not served on the battlefield how can he possibly know? The Minister of National Defence does not have to be dependent upon just half a dozen advisers. My respect for generals is very great, but they are human beings like the rest of us and can make errors. They have made them in every campaign that was ever conducted.
I suggest to the Minister of National Defence that if he wants to get the complete picture on this he does not have to accept my word for it. I quite appreciate that the former minister did not. Let the minister consult with men who had actual experience on the battlefield. Let him consult with lieutenants, captains and majors who went into battle in tanks or in armoured personnel carriers. They are the men who can give him the proper picture. Let him talk to the officers who commanded the Royal 22nd regiment in March and April of 1945 about the use of the armoured personnel carrier. Let him consult with the surviving officers of the Lake Superior regiment who used the armoured personnel carrier at the Hochwald forest. Let him consult with the officers and sergeants and privates of the 54 battalions of British and Canadian regiments who became familiar with the use of the armoured personnel carrier on active service. Let these men give the minister their conception of what it meant. Do not take the word of anyone who did not have that type of experience.
People who were in high command and saw these actions performed from a distance may have a different conception than I have, or some of the men I have mentioned. It is up to the minister if he has, as I am sure he has, the interests of our defence services at heart to the extent that he will not only make them an effective fighting force but will save their lives, to investigate this matter as fully as he can and get the experience of other countries.
He may find a conflict of evidence, because for the 20 years between the two wars the use of armour was brushed aside by those in high command. They did not understand it. When the time came in 1940 to make use of armour they did not understand it and misused it on many battlefields. I do not want 50433-349J
Supply-National Defence to delay the house, but I could name the engagements in which armour was misused. You cannot go by the statements of some men who saw armour misused and therefore would say it is useless. In 1916, in the first world war, the tank was used in the wrong way at the wrong time and on the wrong ground, and was dismissed as a proper weapon for war. It was used properly and successfully at the battle of Cambrai in the fall of 1917. From that experience the use of the tank was developed in 1918. There were many actions in the second world war when the tank was improperly used.
It is the summation of all the evidence that has to be arrived at before a person can reach a conclusion. I cannot see how anyone presently in the army can deny that armour established itself in the second world war, can deny that armour has become a large part of the armies of the great powers of this world, can deny that armour should be maintained within the Canadian army as a component of that force on the basis of equality with the other parts of the service.
If that is not being done-and I believe it is not-the matter should be investigated. I do not wish to pursue this subject here year after year and cause distress to ministers of national defence, but I feel compelled to do it because of the knowledge I have that it is through the use of armour that the lives of men are saved. If there is another war in the near future and Canadian troops are committed to that war, travelling on their feet as they did in the first and second world wars without the protection afforded by armour, my voice will not be stilled.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall we proceed to the next item?
Is the minister going to say anything on this subject?

This is the third time the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre has made a speech on this subject. He raised it on the first day of the debate, and in reply I told him that I had listened to his arguments closely and would be glad to review the circumstances and look into them. Today on two occasions he has repeated the same argument. I do not suppose I can do better than to repeat the same answer.

Mr. Chairman, whilst it is difficult to conduct an argument against complete immobility, nevertheless there are reasons why there should be further emphasis on what has been said in the hope that some of this at least will leave its effect upon the

Supply-National Defence advisers, if not upon the minister himself. I hope it will leave its effect on the minister, but there is one aspect of this situation which is truly alarming.
Here we are in the year 1955, at a time when we have been told, in relation to another discussion, of the ominous events that could happen. Yet in regard to one of the most vital features of any modern fighting force, whether airborne or otherwise, we have really no information at all as to the intention of the government, and particularly as to the intention of the Department of National Defence.
As was pointed out by the hon. member who has just spoken, tanks can now be airborne. As far as the European armies are concerned, and particularly the army of the United Kingdom, the plans contemplate airborne armour being used to a considerable extent. The remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre are made with all the depth of feeling of a man who in two wars has seen the impact of armour upon modern military history. They are made by a man who probably knows more about armour from his own personal experience than anybody in this chamber. In fact I am sure he does.
He made one remark that bears consideration. He spoke about the difficulties confronting the minister if he were in conflict with his advisers. Let us hope the minister is going to be in conflict with his advisers. If there is one fundamental proposition in our whole idea of defence in the democracies, it is that the elected representatives have the responsibility and must accept the responsibility. In that respect there is no question about the right and the duty of the government at any time to make sure that statements of policy shall not be made by senior army officers or members of the staff. But here we have the perfect example of where the minister should assert himself if, in fact, his advisers are suggesting that he go slow in regard to armour.
There could be no more illuminating example offered us in regard to this very subject than the use of the first tanks in 1916. Before the war Churchill, with the imagination which characterized his approach to public affairs at all times, saw the possibilities of tracked vehicles. He did his utmost to persuade the professional soldiers that they should inaugurate a construction program of armoured vehicles using the track system. This was turned down as theoretical and impractical. Later he did succeed in actually having a model built, which was submitted to tests by the army which could not have


been met by any tank built during the first world war. Again the army experts turned down the tank as being impractical for the second time.
Then Churchill, with the ingenuity that has characterized many of the things he has done, himself started the construction of tanks. At that time he was the civil lord of the admiralty. He did a rather irregular thing, which I assume might have got him into trouble. He created a department of land battleships in the navy, and gave instructions for the construction of 18 tanks. Those were built on the basis of plans worked out by the navy. It was as a result of this that the most decisive weapon of the first world war was actually put in the field. It was because he disregarded the advice of the experts that Britain was able to turn the tide with the tanks. People today should reread Ludendorff's "History of the First World War" and recall that he described the 8th of August, 1918, as the blackest day of all, when the British supremacy in tanks decided the fate of the whole battle.
That came from the decision that it is the job of the civil authorities to assert their judgment, having due regard to the advice of their experts. I should like to hear something said here today that would suggest that we are going to have an assertion of that authority by our civil authorities, because it would appear that the things that are being done are too much of an acceptance of the unchallenged advice of experts with whom, apparently, the government has not agreed on a number of occasions on other matters.
I think it applies not only to armour but to everything else we have been discussing. We are still left completely in the dark as to what the plans of the government are with regard to armour. Reread the white paper. There is nothing in it that informs the members of this house or the people of Canada what this government really intends to do. There is confusion of policy; and where there is any sign of policy it has obviously misled the officers themselves, because we have seen the conflict of statements by senior officers in the different services.
As an example, the talk of the trend toward a single continental command undoubtedly represented the thinking of some part of the staff. Other public statements that were made unquestionably represented the thinking of other members of the staff. All this is the result of the absence of any clear policy which will guide either the armed forces or parliament, to say nothing of the public generally. I think what we need above

everything else now is a clear statement of policy by the government as to what it proposes to do to bring our armed forces up to date and in keeping with the demands of the times.
The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, a gallant soldier-a man who has been a professional as well as an amateur soldier-has pointed out that in a large measure we are still organizing and training our army in the same formations as those employed in the battles of the first world war and again in the battles of the second world war. What clearer statement could there be by the most highly qualified soldier in this house that we simply have not moved with the times and that the government is giving us no indication whatever that there has been an adjustment of the thinking of the Department of National Defence and of the government which would assure us that the dollars that are being spent are being spent appropriately?
The discussion which has taken place here today has indicated the difficulty of dealing effectively with estimates in committee of supply here in this chamber. I hope next year the Minister of National Defence himself will urge that the estimates of the Department of National Defence be placed before the committee on estimates, and also that he will urge that the committee on estimates be permitted to deal effectively with this question and not subjected to the limitations that were imposed upon it this year. I would hope that the committee on estimates would be permitted to deal with the estimates of the Department of National Defence with the same authority that is given to a similar committee at Westminster, where the members can bring senior officers before it and where they can call for the production of books and other information not actually subject to the terms of official secrecy. In that way we would meet here with some opportunity to pass judgment with real facts in our possession. As the situation is now, we must admit frankly we have nothing but generalities to support the figures before us.
The hon. member for York West asked a question with regard to the item for travelling and removal expenses found at page 328, and which shows an increase from $16,397,000 last year to an estimated $19,127,000 this year. He asked why this increase was taking place. The minister said this was because of the fact that the brigade would be moved back from Germany this year. There was a tremendous movement to and from Korea during the past year, and Korea is a great deal further from Canada than is Germany. Since the beginning of the last
Supply-National Defence fiscal year-that is the beginning of the fiscal year in 1954-these units were moved from Korea: The third battalion of the R.C.R., the third battalion of the Royal 22nd regiment and the second battalion of the Royal Highlanders of Canada. There was a movement from Korea that involved substantial expense. In addition to that there was a movement of NATO units and of other units back and forth.
Mr. Chairman, as evidence of the fact that the figures are available, I think we should have some breakdown of these figures to show why there has been an increase of approximately $3 million in this item for travelling expenses, in view of the fact that two-thirds of the forces are now back from Korea and that we had that substantial movement within that period. I would hope the minister would give us that as evidence that, at least in regard to this item, it is possible for us to get some measure of information.	,[DOT]

First, Mr. Chairman, to deal with the specific question the Leader of the Opposition has just asked with regard te travelling and moving expenses, I would point out these factors. First, the Korean movement was only a one-way movement whereas the rotation of the brigade is a two-brigade movement. Second, the estimate of last year was not adequate by about $1 million to meet the movements of last year. Now, there has been a continuing movement of reinforcements to the brigade in Europe and of wastage from the brigade. The cost of the brigade proceeding to Europe is estimated at $1,176,000, and of the returning of the brigade $1,235,000, which make a total of around $2,400,000, plus the fact that last year's estimate was exceeded by about $1 million. I think that makes up or more than makes up the difference.

Mr. Chairman, if ever a wand was waved without producing any positive answer, it is being done at this moment. I want to point out to the minister, when he talks about it being a one-way movement, that it could not have been entirely a oneway movement. Actually I omitted one unit that was moved during that period. It was the fourth battalion of the Canadian Guards, which came back in December of 1954. In addition to that, the second battalion of the Queen's Own Rifles came back in April of this year. It is perfectly obvious that there must have been some movement the other way as well, because obviously you were moving units there, not just bringing units back. So that does not answer the question at all.
5530	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence Mr. Campney: I have answered most of the question. I would say with regard to the movement to Korea, perhaps I am wrong as to the date of movement of one battalion there. But in the movement to and from Korea, if there were movement to Korea as well as from it, there were no dependents. In the movement to Germany the number of dependents being moved adds very substantially to the cost.

I have pointed out how unsatisfactory it is to deal with this matter in the committee of supply. Surely we can get a better answer than one saying it is very expensive to move dependents there. Surely we can have some figures that really show exactly how this increase of approximately $3 million is made up. If we cannot get that, then we might as well admit that we are being called upon to deal with this enormous expenditure without the figures available in this house at this time.
The figure provided for the movement of dependents to and from the United Kingdom and the continent is given as $3,512,000. I have not it broken down as between outgoing and incoming movements.
Were dependents not being moved the year before?
No. They rotate with the troops. The brigade in Europe is rotated every second year. So far as the Korean movement is concerned, dependents are not affected.

I am not talking about Korea.
I am talking about Europe.

With respect to Europe, the movement of dependents does not operate in the off year. It is hardly noticeable. It is in the year when one brigade is coming home and the other brigade is going overseas. You have a double movement, and they each take their dependents.

Is it not possible for the minister, ill approximate figures of say hundreds of thousands, to tell us what is involved in the movement of the units and in the movement of dependents, so we can at least see how this additional $3 million is arrived at? Otherwise we are simply voting in the dark.

I can give these general figures which might be of interest to the committee. With respect to the reinforcement and rotation of overseas formations, last year the amount for movement to and from Europe was estimated at $1,732,000. This year it is $5,410,000. Last year the amount for movement to or from the Far East was estimated at $3,797,000. This year it will be under 

$2 million. These are the major differences that make the figures greater this year than last. I gave the house the general figure for dependents, but I do not have it broken down as to the brigade going out and the one coming home.

I point out this does not explain it at all. The net difference in the figures that are given here amounts to about $1,700,000, so it does not explain in any way the increase of approximately $3 million. Either the minister is in a position to give us a simple breakdown of the figures that make up these component figures or he cannot. I would have thought that in relation to every one of these figures there would have been a set of figures as a breakdown that could have been given to the house immediately. Otherwise we must simply admit that the failure is not on the part of the opposition but because of a flat refusal on the part of the government to have the information available which we should have when items of this size or of any size are before the house in committee of supply.

further discussion on the army, regular and general?
If we are not going to get an answer on that, then I have another item with which I want to deal.

I gave the Leader of the Opposition the chief figures which made the differences. There are other subitems which also affect the total. Movement expenses in connection with these exercises this year are anticipated to be $1 million greater than last year. I assumed from the opening remarks of the Leader of the Opposition that he was concerned with the expenses of movements overseas, both to and from Europe and to and from Korea.

I cannot make it any clearer than I have tried to make it, but I would have thought when there is an increase of this nature in one of the larger items it would be possible to say this is the way the figures were made up in bulk last year, this is the way they are made up this year, and this is the difference and the explanation for it. Obviously I cannot get that information

so I shall proceed to see if I can obtain any better information with regard to an item on page 329.
Under the general heading of "acquisition and construction of buildings and works" I see an item for construction of buildings and works amounting to $67,500,000. Last year the amount was $48 million. I should like to know what the circumstances are that call for an increase of $19,500,000 in the construction of buildings and works. I would point out this is only one of the several items for the construction of buildings and works, because similar items are also included in the air estimates and in the naval estimates. It was not so very many years ago that this amount was more than we were spending on the whole defence program in Canada. I should like to know what the nature of the change is and what it is that makes up the additional $19,500,000.

The army construction program is approaching its peak. There are two principal factors involved. The first is the construction of Gagetown. For that this year we are estimating $15 million. The remainder of the increase is largely due to the fact that a great number of the home stations, which I mentioned this afternoon, are at their highest point of construction. For example, we are estimating that for home station and other development we will spend at Valcartier this year $4,980,000, at Barriefield, $4,630,000, at Borden, $3,270,000, at London, $3,570,000, at Petawawa, $5,500,000, at Winnipeg, $4,800,000, at Edmonton, $5,600,000, and at other locations lesser amounts amounting in the aggregate to a substantial sum.
Included in the work are station development programs, barracks, the necessary buildings for the home stations, plus married quarters for the troops. Out of a total expenditure of $67,500,000 estimated for army construction, $17 million represents permanent married quarters.
What was spent on Gagetown last year?
I will get that figure in a moment.

There is an item of $10 million here with regard to army pay and allowances. I notice it was also an even $10 million last year. I am struck by the fact that it is an even amount both years. Does that represent the actual amount paid or is that simply a broadly estimated figure?

That is a broadly estimated figure for those two years.
Supply-National Defence
Can the minister tell us what was actually spent last year? It was estimated at $10 million, I understand.
The actual expenditure was $11,040,000.
I do not want to labour the point, but if that amount was spent last year, what is the reason for an estimate of $10 million for the coming year, in view of the increased activities?
It was anticipated-and it is understood that this is in the militia section-
Yes, that is right.

It was anticipated that there would be as a consequence of reorganization a temporary falling off in numbers and that the figure which had been estimated for the previous year would probably be adequate this year.

speechtext: For the assistance of the committee, I wonder if all members would be kind enough so far as possible to confine their questions at the moment to the army, regular and general. Then when that has been disposed of we can go on to the army, reserve, and so on. We could deal with the subheadings in the order in which they come. I believe this would be easier for all members in the committee, and we would be more likely to get answers from the minister because, as I understand it, as the various items are called there will be a rotation of officials. Mr. Chairman, I would like to go back to the speech of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. Perhaps one of my reasons is that, like many other hon. members in the house, I was able to share with him some of the experiences he mentioned. I saw the things that happened in August of 1918. I saw what happened to infantry when they had to go against machine guns unprotected, and I could hardly believe my ears when I heard this afternoon that this kind of thing could happen again. In my ignorance I thought we had gone beyond that stage.
Earlier in the day I suggested that in answer to the powerful statement, as I thought it was, with regard to tanks, made by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, there were two courses open to the minister. One was to say that the statement was wrong, and give his reasons for saying so. The other was to say that it was right, either in whole or in part, and indicate what steps were going to be taken to meet it.
5532	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence
I was wrong in suggesting that those were the only two alternatives, because apparently there is a third-which is to do nothing. As I understand it, the minister says he will consider the matter. That is all we are to get. Does that make sense, Mr. Chairman? Is this an unexpected thing? Is there something new that has cropped up that the minister has to think over, or is it something that is before him and his advisers, potentially at least, every day of the 365 days in the year?
This is a problem which stands out. Surely no one will suggest for one moment that this is not something the minister has had to discuss often, and no doubt very often. Does it make sense? Should we in this committee accept the suggestion that when a powerful statement has been made and questions asked on this very important matter, a matter of first-class importance, all we are to get is that the minister, with all the array of talent he has at his command, with all the expert assistance he has, will only consider it?
Mr. Chairman, that just does not make sense. I do wish to use moderate language. I do not wish to talk about being insulted or flouted or anything like that. I shall content myself by saying that it just does not make sense. This committee should not be sitting at all if it is not going to persist in the demand that it be given some kind of answer on a matter of this importance.
If I am doing the minister an injustice, let him say so. But I still hope, and I urge most strenuously, that before the estimates are passed he will give us a statement, from information which I am sure must be available to him, as to the views of the department on this question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. We have been dealing with resolution 236, under the heading IMr. Macdonnell.1

Canadian army, regular and general. Have we completed our discussion on this portion of the estimates?
The minister was going to bring forward some information in reply to questions I had asked concerning the enrolment and record at the three military colleges.

Mr. Chairman, I have some statistics here which I think might answer the hon. gentleman's question. I have had a statement prepared reviewing the results of each of the colleges for the last year. I should like to read it. All these figures are for the year 1954-55. I shall deal first with the Royal Military College.
In the first year there were 103 students entered. Eighty passed and one withdrew. There were no supplementaries; 22 cadets, or 21-4 per cent, failed. In the second year there were 83 entered; 71 passed; there were no supplementaries and no withdrawals; 12, or 14-5 per cent, failed. In the third year there were 120 entered, of whom 98 passed; 15 had supplementaries. There were no withdrawals; 7, or 5-8 per cent, failed. In the fourth year there were 94 entered, of whom 77 passed; 15 had supplementaries to write; one withdrew; one failed, or 1 [DOT] 1 per cent.
At Royal Roads, in the first year there were 100 entered, of whom 66 passed; 4 withdrew; 30 failed or 30 per cent. In the second year there were 52 entered; 48 passed; no supplementaries; 2 withdrew and 2 failed, or 3-8 per cent.
At College Militaire Royal de Saint Jean, in the preparatory year 129 entered, of whom 71 passed; 24 had supplementaries to write; 8 withdrew; 26, or 20-2 per cent, failed. In the first year at College Militaire Royal 110 were entered, of whom 84 passed; there were no supplementaries; 2 withdrew; 24, or 21-8 per cent, failed. In the second year 36 entered; 28 passed; there were no supplementaries and no withdrawals; 8, or 22-2 per cent, failed.
That is the complete picture of the service colleges as of the last academic year. I might also give these figures which may be of interest to the hon. member. The over-all wastage of the three colleges for 1948 was 27 per cent.
Since 1948?

For 1948. For 1949 it was 26-5 per cent; for 1950, 27 per cent; for 1951, 24 per cent; and for 1952, 23-5 per cent. I have not the figures. I am informed that the average record of passes and failures of our three Canadian service colleges is almost

identical with the average of the major Canadian universities during the same time.

Mr. Chairman, this information has not been given on the basis on which I asked for it. I asked that the minister take the span covered by the course in the case of the Royal Military College-that would mean four years for the class-and follow it through the four years so we would see from the beginning of that class until the end of the four-year course what the record was, and the same way with the others. In the case of College Militaire Royal de Saint-Jean it would mean starting with the class that entered in 1952, in the preparatory year, and following it through the subsequent years. May I have that information?

I am advised by my officials that information in that form is not kept as a matter of course, and it would take a considerable time to work it out, tracing each individual through the two colleges he attended, because most of them go to R.M.C. finally. In the time at our disposal during the dinner hour it was quite impossible, I am advised, to prepare the exact information in the form requested.

This information is of interest so far as it goes. However, information prepared on the basis I asked for will give us, I think, a complete picture. Take a class and follow it through. I thought the basis I suggested was quite fair; that is, take the span of years covered by a course. Assume that the class would have graduated this past month. Let us see from the official registration-in the case of College Militaire Royal de Saint-Jean, three years; in the case of Royal Roads, two years, and in the case of Royal Military College, four years-what happened to the classes year by year.

I am not sure, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member realizes the difficulty involved in trying to get what he wants. For example, a man goes to College Militaire Royal in his preparatory year. The next year he may go to Royal Roads; he may go to the Royal Military College; he may stay at College Militaire Royal. These colleges are integrated. What would have to be done to give the hon. member the analysis he requires would be to take every individual in every college and trace his career for four years.
I suppose it could be done, but it certainly cannot be done in such time that would be of use here because of the fact that the three colleges have different lengths of courses; three years at College Militaire Royal; two at Royal Roads; four at Royal Military College; and the students do transfer a good
Supply-National Defence deal. I merely state this as a fact. It could not be prepared in the time available because they would have to make a complete study of each student for the whole four years for each of the three colleges. While nothing is impossible, this is impossible within any reasonable time limit.

May I ask a question with regard to the figures we have? What is the minister's feeling in regard to the preparatory year at C.M.R? The figures he has just given for the last year seem to indicate that 24 had supplementaries, 8 withdrew, and 26 failed out of a class of 129. I am wondering whether, on the basis of figures like these, any consideration is being given to the qualifications required of applicants, because that seems to be a year that does not compare favourably with the others, either in the same college or in the other two colleges.

The preparatory year-and College Militaire Royal is the only one that has this preparatory year preparing for the equivalent of senior matriculation-and I think any educational institutions will bear this out, is the year where there are a high proportion of failures. However, the prep year, which was a large class, showed 20.2 per cent failures, whereas in the first year at R.M.C. it was 21.4 per cent and at Royal Roads it was somewhat higher.
I would like to observe that the C.M.R. is just getting into its stride. It is an experiment which is working out extremely well. It is the first military college where we have had a prep class to prepare men to enter, as it were. The feeling of the educationalists in my department is that while there are some matters that should be adjusted, and some things that might be improved, as far as we have gone with this college we have done extremely well. That is the view of the experts who advise me.
When the minister speaks of its being an experiment, is he referring to the introduction of the preparatory year?
The introduction of the preparatory year. Neither of the other colleges has a preparatory year.

I am aware of that, but I am just wondering what support the minister finds for his contention that this experiment of a preparatory year has been successful in the face of these figures. The figures for all three colleges for the other years are much more favourable, I think, than the figure for that one preparatory year.
Supply-National Defence

I do know that as a result of this experiment we get a very high percentage of French-Canadian students who ordinarily would not proceed to senior matriculation. Under this scheme they proceed to junior matriculation and work their way through this college and ultimately to Royal Military College and graduation. I cannot agree with the hon. member that a percentage of 20-2 per cent failures in a junior matriculation preparatory class is out of line when compared with the other educational establishments.

I do not wish to prolong this questioning, but the minister is not taking account of the fact that you had only 71 who passed, whereas there were 24 who had supps, eight who withdrew and 26 who failed.

I have no record of how many of the 24 supps in the case of the C.M.R. will ultimately pass and therefore would be added to the 71 who passed in the first instance. We will not know the answer to that until this fall.

I should like to ask a question about a matter which was brought to my attention this week in a letter from a responsible businessman in British Columbia. He tells me that he met a young man from the United Kingdom who had been recruited into the Canadian army in England. Is there some plan under which the Canadian army recruits in the United Kingdom, or how would that English lad get into the Canadian army in England?

I understand that applicants in Great Britain are accepted for our army but only if they have done their compulsory service there and wish to join our service as a volunteer. Such cases are not numerous.

This young lad intimated that he had enlisted at a Canadian recruiting station in England. Is Canada maintaining a recruiting station in England for the Canadian
army?

No. We have in England an office where anyone may obtain information about the services. It is similar to an immigration or other government office. We are not carrying on any active recruiting in Great Britain, but if a person who probably wishes to settle in Canada comes to us and wants to know what are the conditions of service in our forces, we have an office in Britain which is in a position to supply any information that may be required. I understand also that an interested person can have the desired medical examination, to see whether he is physically acceptable.

In effect that is a recruiting station in England, because you have a Canadian officer there and medical officers to examine potential recruits. I presume they are signed on or give some kind of undertaking before they are brought to Canada. Can the minister confirm that such is the case or, if not, what are the actual conditions?

If a man who has completed his service in the United Kingdom comes to our office and says he would like to enlist in one of our services, and if he passes his medical examination and other tests and is found acceptable to our armed services, he is brought out to Canada on the basis of his enlistment. I understand that his fare is paid. I have not the number here, but this is not an incident of great importance. However, the mechanics are as I have said.
How long has this plan been in effect, and what number of men have been recruited in this way?
I understand that the arrangement which now exists has been in effect for four or five years. I have not the number at the moment but I am endeavouring to get it.
Is a similar plan in effect on the continent? Is it possible for a young man in any of the continental countries to enlist in the Canadian forces?

I understand that where it has been indicated that there are a sufficient number of men in friendly countries on the continent who would like to enlist, arrangements have been made for medical examinations and the obtaining of the relevant data from them. I understand this happened a couple of years ago in connection with the recruiting of bandsmen in Holland. But these are isolated cases and are not of any particular moment as to the number involved.

I am not worrying so much at the moment about the number. I simply would like an explanation from the minister as to why the Canadian government has adopted a policy of enlisting recruits for the Canadian army in the United Kingdom and on the continent.

If persons of a friendly nation wish to join the Canadian forces and they are eligible there is no reason why we should not accept them. That has been the practice, as I say, for the last four or five years. An officer has been established in England continuously. In other places arrangements are made whenever there seems to be a group of suitable persons wishing to join the Canadian services.
Does that not mean that the Canadian army is recruiting mercenaries?

You can use the word "mercenary" in a number of senses. The reason we are anxious to accept these people who offer themselves voluntarily is, first of all, that we believe they will make acceptable soldiers and, second, they will in all probability become settlers in Canada and part of our own Canadian people. If they want to join our army it is usually because they have an interest in Canada. Of course, they will probably not stay in the army all their lives and we hope they will locate ultimately in Canada.
Are they under any obligation to remain in Canada once they have completed their term of service?
No.
Then surely they are mercenaries pure and simple. Why is the Canadian army not filled with Canadian citizens?

For all practical purposes, it is. I do not want to have this minor feature of the Canadian army magnified into a major one, because it is not. And I do not particularly like the word "mercenary". I suppose that every soldier is a mercenary in the sense of being paid. He is paid and he has a right to be paid. I do not know whether the word "mercenary" should be applied to these cases. Our immigration department is looking for good citizens. If a man wants to join the Canadian army and he is physically fit and passes whatever tests are applied, there should be no opprobrium either on him or on the Canadian army which accepts him. After all, we are all in NATO together. We do not seek to persuade these men to join the army. They come of their own volition or they do not come at all.

The Canadian government
apparently is facilitating the enlistment of people from other countries in the Canadian army. It seems to me this is a policy which should have been announced in this house when it was first adopted. Is it possible for a young German to enlist in the Canadian army?
I am informed it was not the case prior to the entry of Germany into NATO. I have no information that the question has arisen since.

Is the government policy such that it would be impossible for a young German to enlist in the Canadian army in the same manner that young men from other continental countries have been enlisting?
Supply-National Defence

It is not impossible now, I would say, but I have not had any application or any suggestion of that sort come to my attention. It certainly was not possible before the admission of Germany into NATO. But now that Germany has been admitted to NATO, if the matter came before me it would have to be considered.
Would young Germans be accepted now?

That would depend on the circumstances of the case and, I presume, to a certain extent on the attitude of the German government. I am not going to make a hypothetical decision because, as I say, the matter has not arisen. If it does I shall have to deal with it, but I would not want to give a categorical answer to a hypothetical question.

I presume one big attraction is the fact that the Canadian pay is considerably higher than these men could get if they enlisted in the forces in their own country. Is that an accurate summing up of the situation?

I would think the principal reason for any person in Great Britain or in Europe approaching us with a view to joining the forces would be that he would want to come to Canada. That would be, I should think, his first motive. One of his reasons for feeling that way would be that if we accepted him into the army or into any service, it would facilitate the movement of his family to Canada. In other words he must have a motive other than just money, I should think. It is true that the pay of Canadian soldiers, as in the case of other wage rates in Canada, is higher than it is in continental countries, but we feel that one of the prime motives for people who wish to join the Canadian forces from abroad is that they want to come to Canada and bring their families to Canada.
