speechtext:
Shall we pass to Canadian
army, militia, at page 329?

On a matter of Canadian army, militia, I have a few comments I should like to make. The hon. member for Colchester-Hants spoke briefly this afternoon on the wrong item in connection with that matter, but I should like to refer to what he said and perhaps amplify it a little.
We are dealing here with a situation in the reserve army which is of paramount importance to many people in the province of Nova Scotia. For a moment I wish to give the background of the situation so the committee can properly appreciate what is being

Supply-National Defence done. We have had in Nova Scotia, which of course maintains the highland tradition, being of Scottish origin, three highland regiments, the North Nova Scotia Highlanders, the Pictou County Highlanders and the Cape Breton Highlanders. Of those the North Nova Scotia Highlanders and the Cape Breton Highlanders both served overseas in the last war. As the hon. member for Colchester-Hants said this afternoon, I do not suppose there is any other battalion with a better record than the North Nova Scotia Highlanders, who went ashore on D-day in Normandy.
The department-and quite properly, because it was urged from all parts of the house-felt that there should be some reorganization of the reserve army. With the principle of reorganization as such no one can have any quarrel whatsoever, but in Nova Scotia the officers and men of these reserve battalions were faced with a problem. They were told by the department that instead of there being three regiments which had heretofore existed with their long traditions, there would have to be ultimately only two. Incidentally the Pictou County Highlanders, although they had not been overseas as a unit, are one of the oldest units in Canada, are associated with the Seaforth Highlanders in the old country, and have a tradition and a record running back over a century.
It was put up to these three battalions that there had to be this reorganization of the reserve army. Many discussions went on among the officers of the battalions, the people in the communities in that whole northeastern part of the province of Nova Scotia who were interested, and officers from the eastern command. It was understood, rightly or wrongly -and apparently wrongly-that if some system could be worked out whereby we could merge with only two battalions instead of three, that would be satisfactory to national defence headquarters and to the officers representing the department in the eastern command.
So the men and officers of these various units worked out what they thought was a satisfactory compromise whereby instead of having the three which had heretofore existed there would be only two, and we would have the Cape Breton Highlanders maintained practically intact with their tartan, their badges and all the rest of it. That would be one of the two regiments which were left. Then you would have the second regiment, which would really be a combination of the North Nova Scotia Highlanders and the Pictou County Highlanders. They were to amalgamate. They would maintain the name of the 
North Nova Scotia Highlanders, which as I said had served in France in the last war, and they would adopt the tartan of the Pictou County Highlanders with the Mackenzie plaid and a lot of the traditions of that old regiment.
That proposition was put up to the Department of National Defence and they said they thought if they could get two regiments, that was all that was required. But later they were told that was not good enough, that we had to scrap the names of the units, we had to scrap the traditions and the badges and everything under the sun, and we were going to end up with a first and second battalion of Nova Scotia Highlanders. They were given the privilege, I think, of choosing a plaid. I see my friend the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough nodding his head. They were given the privilege of choosing a plaid, and I think it was suggested that perhaps they could choose the Nova Scotia plaid.
I have on a tie tonight which closely resembles the Nova Scotia plaid. One of the objections which the officers and men took to it was that about the only description you could give it was that of baby blue; and they thought baby blue was hardly a fair description to give the plaid that would be adopted by these three battalions with these ancient traditions and these old names.
It is something the same as if you took, shall I say, the 48th Highlanders of Toronto, the Toronto Irish and the Toronto Scottish.
I wonder what would have happened if Department of National Defence headquarters had said to them, "You are going to scrap those names; you are going to scrap the traditions; you are going to scrap the badges; you are going to scrap everything, and we are going to clothe you in Hudson's Bay blankets". I think the reaction in Toronto would not have been one of entire, enthusiastic approval. Yet it is exactly the same proposition which has been put up to the men of the North Nova Scotia Highlanders, the Pictou County Highlanders and the Cape Breton Highlanders.
-^s I said, the proposition originally was, "You have to reduce from three to two", and they were prepared to do so. They made the proposition for the merging of the Pictou County Highlanders and the North Nova Scotia Highlanders, which would have meant one regiment in Nova Scotia and the Cape Breton Highlanders would have remained virtually intact in Cape Breton island. But they were told "no".
I think there has been a great deal of doubt about this matter and I am raising it now because I believe the minister can perhaps

still deal with this situation. I doubt whether any firm decision has been made with respect to it. There has been a great deal of "waffling", to use a slang expression. There has been a great deal of indecision and a great deal of uncertainty. No one knows just where he stands. The officers were told, for instance, "You can wear your old uniforms; you can wear your old badges; you can wear your old plaids; we are not going to change those at all; just keep them". In the end you are going to get a battalion which will be clothed like Joseph in coats of many colours, because apparently you can maintain the traditions if you were there previously but if you came in afterwards you are going to have something else.
To say the least it has caused a great deal of uncertainty and a great deal of dissatisfaction in so far as the officers and men of these units are concerned. I think the minister will agree with this. We were talking here about traditions a little while ago. If there is one element more important than another in the maintenance of interest, loyalty and enthusiasm in the reserve army, it is the maintenance of the traditions of the past, the loyalty of the units and all the other matters which are interwoven in the history of battalions and regiments which have been acting together throughout many years. All these presumably are to be scrapped, and we are now being told that we are the experimental ground for a regimental team, whatever a regimental team may be. We are going to have the first battalion of a regimental team and we are going to have the second battalion of a regimental team; but the traditions and the rest of it, as I said, are largely gone.
As a result of this the men in these units are feeling very unhappy. While I am speaking about traditions of the North Nova Scotia Highlanders, may I say that during these last two years the citizens in the towns which are served by that particular regiment have raised over $16,000 for the purchase of uniforms for the officers, N.C.O.'s and the men of that battalion. Now that is to go for naught if this reorganization goes through in the way it was originally proposed. Pictou county, with its record of enlistment, with its traditions and with the money which has been raised there for the support of the Pictou County Highlanders, would lose all that. As I say, you end up with a first and second battalion of a Nova Scotia regiment, but the names and all the matters which have gone into the background have been lost.
I should like to know just why the maritime provinces have been compelled to go through this experience. I think the hon. member for Saint John-Albert has a similar
Supply-National Defence story to tell about New Brunswick. I should like to know in how many other places in Canada this has been done. My understanding-and I could be wrong-is that only two battalions that served overseas, other than those in the maritimes, have been compelled to go through an experience such as this. The minister can tell us how many there are, and before we get through this item I expect he will tell us in just how many places in Canada these so-called regimental teams have been improvised to take the place of old battalions and regiments which served in the past.
You have now a picture of a North Nova Scotia battalion or regiment merged with the Pictou County Highlanders and stretching from Amherst all the way to the strait of Canso, over 200 miles. They have six companies, and the Department of National Defence says it will be perfectly all right if they can organize a couple of more companies. That is fine; they would welcome the companies. We are going to have a regiment with eight companies, and we are going to have a paymaster for them. When my leader was talking today he spoke about having a flying box car to transport troops. The paymaster will have to fly in a helicopter in order to get from company to company to pay them, because they are widely separated.
If you are setting up battalion teams with eight companies stretching over an area of over 200 miles, why in the name of common sense could you not maintain the two battalions they had originally, and which have been there for years and years? But even if that cannot be done I submit that the suggestion of the officers of these units should be accepted. At their own expense, with the great sacrifice and inconvenience which reserve officers put into these units, they have worked out a proposition for merging these two battalions, maintaining the name of one and the tartan of the other, thereby at least keeping alive a semblance of the traditions and records of which all Nova Scotians are proud, particularly those in that area stretching all the way over the northeastern part of Nova Scotia, including Colchester county, Cumberland county, Pictou county, Anti-gonish and Guysborough counties and the island of Cape Breton.
That is a matter which I think should be reconsidered by the minister. I know he will say, as he has probably been advised, that a commission of generals interviewed the reserve officers and got their approval. I am told by those same reserve officers that they never saw this commission of generals at any time or at any place, and that this thing was done without their knowledge and without their consent. I can tell you that it is
5538	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence disapproved of 100 per cent by the officers and men in these units, and by the public who have supported them. Surely if the minister is going to make a success of the reorganization of the reserve army he has to conserve the traditions, the records, the uniforms, the badges and all the things that go with the intangibles to create sentiment, loyalty and patriotism. That is all being scrapped for this rather mechanical device of a first and second battalion of a Nova Scotia regiment.
I am sure there is no documentation to prove it, but I am even told that somebody thought-one of these nebulous suggestions that come down through the grapevine-that if the officers of the two battalions would accept this they could even get the word "royal" so it would be the Royal Nova Scotia Highlanders. I thought, of course, that "royal" was a word which had gone out of fashion and was in ill repute, but apparently it could be obtained by these men if they were prepared to enter into this so-called regimental team.
That, Mr. Chairman, is for the moment the background of this matter. It is one I have no hesitation at all in raising because, though I do not come from a constituency directly affected by it, I have had representations from scores of officers who are involved in these battalions, and it is a matter of interest to the whole province of Nova Scotia.
I am told by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert that the same experience has been had by the battalions in the province of New Brunswick. Before this item is passed I want to know just what has been done in other places, where this matter stands at the moment, and what the minister thinks might be done to maintain the esprit de corps which, as I said, I think is the most valuable part of any unit, particularly a defence unit and which, I suggest with all deference to him, is going to be largely lost if this mechanical reorganization being insisted upon by certain people is carried into effect.

Mr. Chairman, I have been waiting all afternoon and evening for this item in order to say what the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings has said. He has said it so much better than I could have that I am not going to take the time of the committee to repeat much of what he has said. I probably would have said it with adjectives which would not look good in print and which the hon. member contained himself enough not to use, but I do say emphatically that things are in a bad way in north and northeastern Nova Scotia,
TMr. Nowlan.]

which takes in Cumberland, Colchester, Anti-gonish, Guysborough and the island of Cape Breton.
I happen to have been associated with the Pictou Highlanders, an outfit which, according to rumour, is going to be scrapped, and I can tell the minister that by word of mouth from those living in my riding and by letters -I suppose I have a file as thick as my fist- I have received complaints not only from the Pictou Highlanders but from the northern portion of Nova Scotia and Cape Breton, and so have other members from those areas.
I have taken up the matter with the minister by letter, but I do want to endorse most emphatically what the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings has said, and said so much better than I could. I am not going to take any more time to try to impress upon the minister that this is something to which he had better give a second look.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to support what the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings and the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough have said. I rise particularly at this time because I had some contact with the North Nova Scotia Highlanders during the war, and I think to do such a thing to a regiment with traditions as fine as it has and which fought as gallantly as it did is just unbelievable. I had some experience in the militia before the war and after the war.
I know, I am sure the minister knows, and anybody who has been in the militia knows, that the whole strength of a militia regiment lies in its traditions. The pay is insignificant. It is the traditions of the regiment, the spirit, the esprit de corps, as the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings has said, that make or break a regiment. If you have it you have a regiment. If you do not have it you have nothing. They do not go there for the pay. They do not go there for any other reason except that they believe in the spirit and the traditions.
I believe it is utter stupidity to make these two fine regiments into the first and second battalions of the Nova Scotia regiment. What does that mean to them? It means nothing. You might as well call them X and Y battalions. It is like putting numbers on a can of beans. The things that have meaning to a militia regiment are their uniform, their battle honours, their traditions. Once you give them a new name they lose all these things. They do not carry them along with them. They become a new battalion and the traditions and esprit de corps vanish.
I was a member of the 48th Highlanders of Toronto. I can imagine what would happen

to the esprit de corps of that fine regiment if they were called the first, second or third battalion of the Ontario Highlanders. There would be utter disgust, and you would lose what makes one of the great regiments of this country.
I am also disturbed about what appears to be happening to another great Toronto militia regiment, the Queen's Own. I understand that their recruiting base has been shifted to Calgary, which to me sounds absolutely fantastic. The Queen's Own is a Toronto regiment and has been for many many years. It is one of the really old battalions of this country. Its roots are in Toronto, its spirit is in Toronto, its alumni are in Toronto, and if you want to raise men for the Queen's Own you had better leave the recruiting base in or near Toronto so the traditions of that regiment can remain intact.
I think the treatment of the militia by the government at the present time and the creation of the first, second, third and fourth Guards battalions is stupid. Why not leave these fine regiments intact with their traditions and names that mean so much to them? Why not leave them with the most important things they possess, their uniforms, their names, their traditions? Why do what bureaucrats are always trying to do, streamline or simplify, and in so doing complicate and lose what originally was possessed?
As a former member of the militia and knowing how much these things mean, I appeal to the minister to stop what I consider to be this stupid process of destroying the really important things that keep a militia regiment going, and the only things that do. Leave them intact. Let our regiments remain the fine regiments they are, with the fine traditions they have had for many years past.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak on the same subject with particular reference to New Brunswick. I am a little hesitant, in that my sole contribution on the defence estimates has to be directed to a new minister who is perhaps not entirely responsible for the action that has been referred to; nevertheless it is still within his powers to remedy the situation.
I took the opportunity to refer to the discrimination against maritime units during the throne speech debate, and I do not wish to go over the details of the story, but there are one or two pertinent facts that I think should be mentioned this evening. You know, when these various discriminations take place against the maritimes, quite often we are told when we approach Ottawa, "Oh, you should have told us that before. We would have been glad to accommodate you at the time,
Supply-National Defence but it is too late now." First of all I would like to point out that we were in this thing, very early, in the beginning, and we foresaw this discrimination and these changes that were coming.
Last year on May 6 I placed a question on the order paper, before the so-called Kennedy report was published. In fact I doubt whether at that time the entire investigation had been completed. These were the questions I asked on May 6th:
1.	(a) Are reserve force Infantry units classified A, B, C, etc.?
(b) What are the classifications of the respective-reserve force infantry units in Canada.
2.	(a) What were the strengths of the respective reserve force infantry units in summer camps in 1953?
(b) What were the strengths of the respective reserve force infantry brigades in summer camps in 1953?
3.	What are the strengths of the respective reserve force infantry units in Canada at the present time?
The point of placing those questions on the order paper was that we knew these changes were coming up, and we suspected from the very beginning that there was going to be the usual discrimination against the maritimes. We decided to get our oar in first, this time. So that question was placed on the order paper, at the suggestion of many of the reserve force officers in the Saint John area who wanted to point out that their units were up to scratch. They had always been told their recruiting and their strength at camp was good. Perhaps the true test is the fact that the appointments and the other space that is given to units in the various orders and military journals always contained a large proportion of members of these New Brunswick and other maritime units.
That was all they had to go by, except the word that had been given to them by visiting, colonels and the like. That question was not answered. It went to the head of the order paper, and it was at the head of the order paper for one full month; then died at the end of the session.
I suggest tonight that perhaps there was; some reason for not answering all the details, because the report was still in process of examination. But I want to point out that the idea was to establish our position early, in the beginning, so we would not hear the same old story, "Oh, you are too late." We did not want to have that levelled against us again.
Well, what happened? We found out from various sources, through the dribble-drabble of information that comes down our way,, that these major generals-Kennedy, Letson and Renaud-did visit New Brunswick, and they were there for two hours. And it is on
5540	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence record, at least among the officers around my area, that they spent the two hours in a mess talking to the other officers who were there. There is no possible way they could have obtained first-hand information. But they did visit New Brunswick. 1 do not know whether they got as far as Nova Scotia. I do repeat that they were in New Brunswick, but only for two hours, enjoying the pleasantries of the mess.
The report came out, and there is a point I would like to stress, because it has not been carefully explained in the letters we have had from the department. There are thick files in the messes in New Brunswick, and I have a thick file here, myself. The story is not that we object-and we did not object at the time-to the reduction in the number of battalions. We had three battalions in New Brunswick, and three reserve force battalions were in existence in Nova Scotia.
If the department can produce figures here this evening to show that our strength, our recruiting, and our activities at camp do not warrant three battalions when compared with all the other units in Canada, that is perfectly all right with us. We do not object to a reduction from three to two. But, Mr. Chairman, the thing we do object to-and may I say no note has been taken of it in any of the replies I have had from the department -is that there was no need to discriminate against us in the names of the regiments in the maritimes. To my knowledge it was not done anywhere else in Canada.
Tonight I am going to throw some questions to the minister, and I do really wish he would take time this evening, if he has the information, to clear the air on this entire reorganization scheme. For example, I would like a statement telling me how long the generals were in New Brunswick, and the information they obtained. I would like a statement on the strength of the units, classifying them under the old A, B, C system or any other way he likes. I would like to know why it was necessary to wipe out completely the three regiments.
As I have said, I do not know of any other area, other than Nova Scotia, in which this was done. We do not object to the reduction; it is simply the fact that we lost the names of two of our oldest, historic regiments. Mention was made in the discussion this evening of the Queen's Own Rifles. I do not think anybody would say anything against the fine record that regiment has had. One hon. member referred back as far as the Fenian raids.
Mr. Chairman, we go back to 1793 with our regiment; and the ironical fact about the whole thing is that in 1793 we had a regiment called the New Brunswick regiment. So we IMr. Bell.]

are right back to where we were in 1793. And that is so because the department, or whoever was responsible for this decision, in its wisdom has decided that they will wipe out the names of all our old regiments and call them first New Brunswick regiment, brackets, Carleton-York, and the second New Brunswick regiment, brackets, north shore. Why all these brackets? Is the idea just to ease us into the situation and kid us along about the whole thing? Already I have had my mess bill from the first New Brunswick, Carleton-York regiment-and you cannot even see the "Carleton-York", it is in such small print.
I saw a letter the other day from the department about dress, what the regiment will do with the kilts which arrived on the boat from England on the day they disbanded the unit. I had a letter from the department, and in the letter to me they have called it the New Brunswick regiment; and either they forgot or purposely they did not put in any of the brackets.
It just does not add up, so far as I am concerned. The only thing I can see about it, the only good that could come out of it, in changing our regiment every ten years, or whenever it happens, is that you give us a chance to fill our churches with old battle colours. We are proud of our traditions down there, and we still would like to be able to hold on to some of our names. There is no sense making a report about the New Brunswick and Nova Scotia men, their units, their decorations and all that sort of thing. Everybody in this place knows about the enlistments and all those other things we are so proud of down our way.
But I do want an answer to all these questions. I want to know why it was necessary to wipe out the names of our units when the other units-the Queen's Own, the Black Watch and all the rest of them-were not even touched. I would like to think it was not the result of lobbying or politics, but I am just afraid somebody in the department said, "Oh, the maritimes-they are away down there, out of sight. Maybe there will be a kick or two, but we have to worry about these powerful messes around Toronto and Montreal."
I do say, Mr. Chairman, that we want an explanation about this. The matter is in the hands of the new Minister of National Defence, and we ask him to clarify it, to clear the air. Perhaps we do not have a united stand on the changes as in Nova Scotia, but we are entitled to a complete reinvestigation of the whole matter, and a statement on it.

If nobody else wishes to speak on the militia reorganization, perhaps

I might make a few observations. In the first place, the militia reorganization was instituted at the request of the conference of defence associations in the belief that it was desirable to review the whole situation in Canada and make such adjustments and changes as the facts might warrant. This was not a particularly new departure; it has happened in Canada and probably will happen again. At the request of the conference of defence associations a commission was appointed by the chief of the general staff under the chairmanship of Major General Kennedy to examine the situation and make recommendations. They made that examination and they made their report.
They discussed all their problems with the conference of defence associations, and they discussed specific changes with all general officers commanding and the chairman of the conference of defence associations. Let me say at once that there were no politics whatever in connection with these discussions and these decisions and there was no suggestion of politics that I ever heard of until it was implied here this evening.
I should like to say also there has been no discrimination against the maritimes, as I think I shall show in a moment. One of the things the committee recommended was that we should have fewer infantry regiments, and that we should have more of certain other arms of the service. As a matter of fact they recommended the conversion of three infantry regiments to armour. That might be regarded as proof that some of the views of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre had registered. In any event, after reviewing all the facts they decided there should be across Canada 13 fewer infantry battalions.
Then, after a study of all of the factors that were relevant, three battalions which had theretofore been infantry battalions were as I have said converted to armour; and ten lost their identity. The location of those regiments which lost their identity was as follows: one in Alberta; one in Manitoba; four in Ontario; three in Quebec; one in Nova Scotia; and one in New Brunswick. Therefore I do not think any person in any part of Canada can properly level a charge of discrimination, because the changes that were made were made generally across the country, and in a general way somewhat in accordance with the population of those areas.
Now, as to the two provinces whose representatives have made representations here this evening, I think a parallel situation exists in respect of each. It was the feeling of the general officers commanding and the chief of the general staff that, having regard
Supply-National Defence to all the relevant facts, the two provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick could each adequately support two battalions. So far as Nova Scotia is concerned, I would hesitate to get immersed in the battle of the tartans. I have only a very remote claim to the use of the Crawford tartan, but it is not involved in this particular struggle.
The reason it was felt there should be two battalions in each of these provinces, each battalion having in part the same name, that is a name identified with the province, was that in the event of a war it would be far better to have two battalions in which the personnel would be interchangeable and which would be known, in one case as the Nova Scotia regiment and in the other, the New Brunswick regiment. It is well known,
I think, to all members that in both the last two wars the transfer of recruits and of men from one regiment to another and the disbanding of certain regiments during the war presented real difficulties. When the war was over certain battalions from local areas had great numbers of personnel from other parts of Canada acquired during the war.
There is a feeling in the general staff that if we could have, as we have in the regular army, two battalions to one regiment, or three battalions as the case may be, where it is possible, it would be an excellent idea from the point of view of identity of the fighting troops with the areas from which they come and from which they would draw recruits.
The feeling was that there should be one battalion for Nova Scotia on Cape Breton island and one on the mainland. The two-battalions perpetuate the names of the two battalions which went overseas. In the case of New Brunswick the idea was to have two battalions of the New Brunswick regiment, and in doing so the identity of the old battalions was lost in part. There was some discussion about this at the time, but not a great deal. As a matter of fact there was some discussion about several battalions across the country, because every time you change the accepted order of things, there are people who are not inclined to favour such changes. But I must say that since I came into office a year ago the changes that were made-and they were quite numerous-have been very well received throughout the country. I can think of only two or three cases where there was any particular agitation.
As I have said, representations were made-from New Brunswick and from Nova Scotia. They were all reviewed. I understand various meetings were held locally but in the end, so far as I have known, until tonight, the arrangement that was made in these two provinces was not seriously questioned at
5542	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence the time. It seems to me that, since the battle honours of all these battalions will be retained, and since the net effect of these changes is to consolidate provincial feelings around two battalions of a provincial regiment, that if the supporters of these battalions would do as they have done in almost every other case in Canada, and get behind those battalions they will really be amazed at what they can do to build two strong, active battalions in each province.
I feel that the matter has been very thoroughly studied and considered. Views have been received and have been considered. It seems to me that perhaps we are putting too much emphasis on battalion names. After all, the spirit of the people and the record in war of these people in the different provinces are the things that make for loyalty to their own provincial or local regiments.
I must reiterate what I said at the beginning, that there was, so far as I know, no attempt or thought of provincial discrimination or of any other type of discrimination that would be to the detriment of the regiments being established in these two provinces.
While I am on my feet perhaps I might refer to some of the observations made this morning about the use of the Connaught ranges. I must say to the hon. member for Broadview that I do not appreciate at all his continual reference to the stupidity of bureaucracy in connection with the requested use of the Connaught ranges by the girl guides.
There was a real reason why this request was not acceded to. I am doing my level best to get the Canadian army extricated from Long Branch. We are studying now what we can do at Camp Borden, to meet the Long Branch situation. We anticipate that for the next year or two the Connaught ranges will be used much more than they have been used in the past. We maintain these ranges primarily for the use of rifle associations and troops. The dominion rifle association meets there in July, and we have had a number of requests for the use of the non-shooting part of the range, which would be involved in this large visitation of girl guides, by cadet units which are growing in number and are receiving fuller training.
On the basis of what we know now we believe that the Connaught ranges will be required to a greater extent in future years than they have been in the past. It may be that we could consider moving up the date of the girl guides' camp. I certainly want to co-operate with the girl guides and with any other national organization which might 

desire our facilities, but I must put military needs first. It was not stupidity of bureaucracy that led to this decision, but the possible military requirements.
Another point was raised by the hon. member for Broadview about recruiting. As he knows, there is a major recruiting base in Toronto and recruits enlisting from the Queen's Own militia regiment or from any other source may specify the Queen's Own regiment, which is now a regular regiment, as the regiment of their choice. That regular regiment has never been stationed in Toronto, as a matter of fact. I should think the people of Toronto might be proud to have the name of one of their militia units, which is favourably known throughout Canada, selected as the name of a regular regiment. There is no disposition not to encourage people from the Queen's Own militia regiment or from the Toronto area indicating that they desire to enlist and be sent to the Queen's Own regiment. People have the choice when enlisting as to the unit in which they wish to serve.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has so many matters to deal with that I can appreciate his reference to the Connaught ranges, the Queen's Own regiment, and the rest of it. For a few minutes I should like him to keep his eye on the ball as far as the maritime provinces are concerned and the references made by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert and myself.
The minister says he never heard of any suggestion of politics until tonight. I am not suggesting for one moment that there were politics with a capital "P".
I absolve the hon. member; the reference to politics was made by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert.

The hon. member for Anti-gonish-Guysborough spoke on this matter, and I want to say that I have the proof in my hand. When you get reserve army officers of the rank of brigadier who are ready to go to the public press and make statements with respect to this matter, one of them a candidate in the election before last, I think it can be said that in Nova Scotia at any rate there is no suggestion of partisan politics.
I think there is a suggestion of politics with a small "p", and that is probably what the hon. member for Saint John-Albert had in mind.
Despite what the minister has said, we in the maritimes feel that there has been some discrimination. I want to have the minister clear that up before we pass this item tonight or a week from tonight or whenever it is

finally passed. The minister referred to the fact that there was a commission which suggested that in so far as Nova Scotia was concerned there should be only two battalions. I am not quarrelling with that at all at the moment. I think the officers in the different regiments felt that perhaps that had to be so. If they had to be reduced to two no one was going to take issue with that.
The issue is, what was the solution? I want to say frankly that I do not think the minister is wholly conversant with the situation. I hope that after this discussion tonight he will review the whole position. The officers and men accepted the proposition that there should be two battalions. They regretted that, of course, but they finally accepted it. But then came the question of how the composition of the two battalions was going to be determined, how the two would operate where hitherto there had been three. That is where the quarrel arises.
The officers and men of these three battalions worked out a solution which met the requirements of the two, and quite frankly they thought that was acceptable to the Department of National Defence and the officer commanding on the east coast. They went away from those conferences feeling that while this was an unfortunate situation, the best solution had been arrived at and they would be able to maintain, as I said, the name of the North Nova Scotias, who had gone overseas, as well as the name and emblem of the Pictou County Highlanders, which was the oldest regiment of the three, and also preserve the name and emblem of the Cape Breton Highlanders. That was their proposition and it met the problem to which the minister referred, that of reducing three to two.
I want to know why that regimental proposal was not accepted instead of having it brushed aside by some person or persons at the top. This commission apparently spent some time at some places in New Brunswick, but I am told they did not spend any time in Nova Scotia. They probably could not find one of those places in Nova Scotia to which my hon. friend referred in New Brunswick. I am advised by the officers commanding these battalions, as well as the other officers, that none of them ever saw this commission or any of the three generals concerned. In fact they never heard of them and did not know they were there except that at Camp Utopia there was a casual conversation about them. That was all they knew about it.
I want to impress upon the minister that our quarrel is not with this reduction from
Supply-National Defence three to two, but is with how the reduction was effected. The minister says that ten regiments in Canada have lost their identity, or 13 as three of them went into another branch of the service. I should like to know the names of the ten, and how many of them had service overseas in the second or the first war. Our information, right or wrong, is that the only ones which had service overseas which have lost their identity were those in the maritime provinces, one in New Brunswick and two in Nova Scotia, and possibly there might be two others in all the rest of Canada.
That information may be wrong, as it is most difficult to get such information. It is unpleasant for any officer associated with the reserve army-I am not suggesting for a moment that any active officers had anything to do with it-to give out information of this kind. The minister says there was only one in Nova Scotia that was reduced, but I say there were three. I suppose you can say there are two left but, as the hon. member for Saint John-Albert said, we lost the North Nova Scotia Highlanders, we lost the Cape Breton Highlanders and we lost the Pictou County Highlanders. Now we have the first battalion (Nova Scotia), and that is in brackets, in fact very small brackets just like the Union Jack in the South African flag. You need a microscope to find it. As the hon. member for Saint John-Albert said, the brackets soon disappeared.
Why should the regimental proposal not be accepted in relation to what is called a regimental team? The minister says there is a provincial tradition. My hon. friend from Winnipeg South Centre says perhaps there is a historian in the Department of National Defence. I have sometimes thought the hon. member for Twillingate and I were the only historians in the house, but perhaps we have one in the Department of National Defence.
I am sure the hon. gentleman would not mind my interrupting, just to correct the pronunciation of Twillingate.

After you get that ferry in Newfoundland you can make the second discovery of it. But I find now to my surprise-[DOT] and my hon. friend from Winnipeg South Centre showed me a history of the regiments of Canada-that there was a Nova Scotia regiment way back around 1750. Apparently the historian is trying to make us feel good by making us adopt his old historical names.
There are various regiments all over the province, but there is no provincial tradition attached to any one regiment. To call it the Nova Scotia regiment does not meet
5544	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence any purpose whatsoever. Therefore I suggest again that I should like an explanation from the minister, and I am not blaming the minister for this at all if it was instituted before he took over this department. Many protests have come in and I think they have been dealt with at other levels, but it is time for the minister to deal with them at the ministerial level. You have a ridiculous situation where to make people feel good you let them wear a uniform. You say, "We will adopt another uniform. If you cannot decide on that, we will decide on it". You get a situation where you destroy the esprit de corps. Perhaps the minister can clear this up tonight. If they have not been discriminated against and this has happened to every battalion, let us be told that.
The officers who were commanding these battalions said the difference between what the national defence department wants them to do and what they want to do is that the national defence department wants to disband all existing units and start off with two new units, with new names and new badges. The officers propose retaining the present unit, with the badges of two of the battalions and the tartan of the third. It would seem to me that this is a reasonable proposal. We feel that the department's proposal abandons all the traditions of these three battalions. On the other hand the regimental proposal maintains all these traditions whilst meeting the requirement to which the minister referred a moment ago, of having only two battalions. That is their suggestion, and the minister can perhaps prove them wrong.
I shall not speak longer on this subject.
I am looking for information, not trying to create a forum where we can declaim about the traditions and the pride of these three battalions. But we want to get more information from the minister before this item finally carries.

Before the minister replies to the questions asked by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, I should like to make two points I did not make clear earlier. First,
I did not want to indicate any sort of partisanship in the sense of political parties, in my complaint against the different messes.
I simply meant to indicate that the larger units, which have been in existence for many years, in Montreal and Toronto have people who are active in the city and have traditions that go away back. Their fathers, grandfathers and so on were in those units, and if anything had been done to them there would have been quite a hue and cry.
I think everybody will admit that in our case we have had the names of our regiments changed so many times since the


Boer war that if your father or grandfather was in one of them, it was a different regiment even though it had a local connection. So there is not the same continuity of history and background at all in our part of the country. If the minister expected that there would be any great outcry from an organized, powerful group over the loss of identity of any of these regiments, he would really be mistaken. The names have been changed so recently that there is perhaps not the same objection to it.
Second, the minister perhaps inadvertently gave a clue to the point we are trying to get home when he said there were ten losses of identity in Canada among the regiments. I believe there were 13 reductions. Our point in New Brunswick, particularly, is that the loss of the names of the regiments is so unnecessary. I myself think today that the officers of the reserve army in the province are probably quite satisfied with the new set-up as regards the location, the new training plans, etc. But we have unnecessarily lost the names of our old regiments.
When he was reporting the fact that there were ten losses of identity in Canada, the minister came to the maritimes and said there was one in New Brunswick and one in Nova Scotia, and then he added "in part". That is the key to the whole thing. We have lost three units in New Brunswick, as far as their names are concerned. It is the same in Nova Scotia. There are eight other changes in Canada. I wish the minister would correct me on this if I am wrong, because that is the whole point of our argument. There were eight other losses of names in Canada besides those in the maritimes, and under this new plan we have lost six. That is my point, Mr. Chairman, and when the minister answers the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings perhaps he could answer that.
I take it you are referring to the names of units, and not to units as such.
The identity of the units as applied to their names.

While the minister is ascertaining that information, may I say on the same point that this is a very interesting evening, in that emphasis has been so effectively placed upon the importance of tradition in the army by the two hon. members who have recently spoken, the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings and the hon. member for Saint John-Albert. After hearing the remarks of those two members I think the minister and his officials will be very careful in the future with regard to interfering with the traditions of units within the forces.

Tradition means much more to service people than some have imagined. Tonight we have had that emphasis very properly placed.
I think part of the trouble has arisen because the report of the commission, which I think was received by the department in January, was not announced to the press until after the House of Commons rose last year, and the fact that the question placed on the order paper by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert was not answered while the house was in session. We were waiting all last session to hear the report on the reorganization of the militia, but it was delayed.
Some of those who have spoken here tonight have suggested that the present minister bears no responsibility. But it occurs to me that he was associate minister of national defence, and perhaps this was the very section of the Department of National Defence that came under his supervision. It would be extremely interesting if that turned out to be the case.
I think we all recognize that reorganization of the militia units in Canada has taken place frequently ever since confederation and is occasionally censured; but when that reorganization takes place, greater attention should be paid to the tradition of the units concerned. The historical members of the house who have been named tonight-and who I think are rather fragile reeds on whom to lean- might direct their attention to the book "Canada's Soldiers, 1604 to 1954" by Lieutenant Colonel Stanley to which 1 have referred previously. There they will get a history of the Canadian militia. I recommend it to the Department of National Defence.
There you will find that Colonel Stanley says that in the various reorganizations which have taken place in the Canadian militia, attention has not been paid to tradition. We would find our present militia regiment battle honours extending much further back than they do had earlier reorganization been done carefully. It is still not too late for someone interested in the project to link the present militia regiments with Canada's past history in so far as the militia is concerned. It is indeed a glorious history of service and sacrifice for this country.
I have one other point to make. The minister said that in this reorganization that has recently taken place people appeared to be satisfied, that they had had no serious complaints, and so on. The minister surely is familiar with the chain of command in the army. It is extremely difficult to get a complaint to the minister. Suppose a lieutenant, a captain or a major is dissatisfied with what is happening to his battalion or his regiment.
Supply-National Defence How in the world is he ever going to get word to the Minister of National Defence? He must go through the chain of command. His colonel must approve of any complaint that goes forward. Then it has to go to the brigadier, to militia headquarters or something like that; and of course it ends up in the waste paper basket, or the man who wants to make a complaint is even eased out of the service. The Minister of National Defence is completely insulated in so far as hearing reports from the militia is concerned.
That is why we are trying to break through and get the minister's attention.

It will take a supersonic plane to pierce the barrier and get through to the Minister of National Defence. You just cannot get through. Consequently he will never hear anything about it and will be able to tell us in the house that everything is all right, that no complaints have been received.
That is what the hon. gentleman thinks.
A great many more think the same thing.

It is only because of freedom of speech in parliament here that the opportunity is given to bring complaints of this nature to the ear of the Minister of National Defence. I felt handicapped when I was in the militia, just about a year ago, and I did not even speak about the militia here in the house. I did not want to run afoul of the general commanding out in the district around Winnipeg. My unit might have suffered. Eventually we parted friends, however.
Nevertheless, that is the real difficulty. Unless matters of this kind are brought to the attention of the minister he will never hear of them. Consequently if he will now proceed with his answers to the questions raised by the two members from the maritimes, I think we will get the desired information. It will then go out to those who are so greatly concerned with regard to the reorganization of the militia. Unless the matter is explained by the minister and is given consideration by him it will cause a bit of trouble within militia units across the country, including those that have been compelled to disband and those that fear being dealt with in the same way.
Will the minister now reassure the regiments across the country that if any further changes are to be made, full attention will be paid to the tradition and the origin of those regiments?
Carried.

Oh, no; it is not carried.

Supply-National Defence

As to the information the hon. member requested, namely the names of the ten units disbanded and the information as to which of those units had been overseas in the last war, may I say that I am waiting for it. It is being prepared, but I do not have it here at the moment.

When the minister is dealing with the matter a little later on, either tonight or at some other time, will he tell the committee why the so-called regimental proposal was rejected in favour of the command proposal, when they both achieve the same result? I refer to the getting of the two battalions, but in one case maintaining all the very best that could be preserved all through and in the other case scrapping everything. I think the minister should give his explanation as to why that was done, for the benefit not only of the committee and of the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough who raised the same matter, but of everyone who is interested.

We have heard about the investigation that was made by the three officers before their findings were put into effect, wiping out the identity of some of these regiments. I wonder whether the minister might inform the house what type of investigation they carried out. That is, will he tell us where they held their meetings, whether they did the investigating here in Ottawa in an office in front of a blackboard or whether they visited the various areas concerned, to whom they talked, and whether they gave an opportunity for the various people interested in those militia units to appear before them and discuss the situation before their findings were made known to the department?

I cannot give my hon. friend the details of the trips and investigations made by the committee. I know they spent several months, most of it in travelling from one side of Canada to the other. I cannot say that they visited every unit or the site of every unit, but I can say that they made a comprehensive survey having been thoroughly briefed before they started and having a good deal of background knowledge of their own with respect to the different areas, the different regiments and the different units.
I can say that it was a thorough and detailed investigation. I cannot go beyond that into a day by day description of where they went and what they did.

In the preamble to the report there must be some record of the places they visited and the number of people whom they interviewed, and something to show whether they called witnesses 

at all in connection with the survey with regard to any individual city or locality in which they held the hearings.

There is a fairly substantial volume of minutes, observations and data on what they did and where they went. I do not have any of that material here, but what I said generally was based on what I have seen in the report. I think that is a fair summation of the activities of the committee.

There is one other question I should like to have answered, in addition to the statement the minister is going to make later about the report itself and the training of the units, along the lines suggested by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings. After the original announcement was made of the reorganization plans as outlined in the Kennedy report, in other words after all the units were renamed, redesignated and reduced in the way it was done, were there any other units which applied or wrote to the department or lobbied and received further consideration as far as names or amalgamations were concerned? Was the plan outlined in the report carried out exactly, or were there one or two further changes made in Quebec or Ontario along the lines of the changes requested by the maritime units?

There were some representations made by some units. It is my recollection that although representations were made, it was a good while before there were any from Nova Scotia or the maritimes generally. I recall one case in Alberta, one in Ontario, and there may have been one or two others, where representations were made and where the local military people got together and worked a compromise which was acceptable to the department. But there were very few such cases. I can think of only two at the moment.
The minister says there were no representations made by the maritime units. There was considerable correspondence, if that can be looked upon as being representations.
Not, I think, for a very considerable time. I stand to be corrected if I am wrong.

I have correspondence of July, 1954. I am sure the minister and the Minister of Labour both got letters at that time. That was just after the announcement was made.
I remember that the units were at camp in the first week of July of 1954 when the announcement of the implementation of the report was made. I hope the minister will reinvestigate the matter, make a further

statement, if possible, and perhaps try to get together with some of the unit commanders to see if something can be done. We certainly feel that the names of our units are going to be discarded unnecessarily because of red tape. It has been admitted by the minister that two concessions at least were made in Ontario and Quebec after the original announcement, and if that was done we certainly feel that we are also entitled to some concession.
Tha Deputy Chairman: Is there anything furtiier under army, militia?

I believe the administration of armouries comes under this particular heading, and I should like to ask the minister a question concerning the use of armouries for general community purposes. More recently, as new armouries have been constructed in Canada, emphasis has been placed on designing them in such a way that they can be used for general community purposes. If that is the case, I should like to ask the minister on what terms are these armouries made available for such purposes?

The disposition of armouries for civilian use in the community rests with the G.O.C. of the district. Where it is a local, community, non-profit effort we collect no rent. We insist that the place be kept clean and tidy, that any expenses necessary for that purpose be met, and usually that fire insurance be placed on the building for the period during which it is being used. Inasmuch as these armouries are primarily built for military purposes, we are anxious to limit other use to community purposes. For noncommunity profit-making uses, we would make a substantial charge.

I should like to place a
specific example before the minister. Would he consider a flower show by a horticultural society a legitimate community effort open to the concessions he has outlined?

I would not like to express an opinion on the case the hon. member has put forward, because there would be other facts that would have to be known. If it was a local institution which the whole community was supporting and there was no thought of some party or parties making a profit, it would seem to me it might come within that category. On the other hand, a flower show might be held with the idea of making some profit and with only a very small section of the community having any interest in it. In that case I think the G.O.C. would have to look at the matter.
Supply-National Defence
Each case that arises-and we have quite a number of them-has to be looked at sensibly on its merits. On the one hand we do not want to encourage the use of armouries for private, money-making purposes. And we must keep them available for such military needs as require to be met. But I think generally speaking we get on pretty well with the people who wish to use the armouries for community purposes, and we try to be cooperative and work with them.

I was interested in what the previous speaker had to say on this item, and I want to make a few comments. The newer armouries that have been built in recent years are of a good type and design. They are of excellent construction, are spacious and permit exercises under cover and things of that sort. In some communities there are excellent corps of naval cadets, army cadets and air cadets, and a great deal of interest is shown by some people in building up these organizations. I know that in my own district those responsible are entitled to a great deal of credit for what they have done.
The armouries come under the entire jurisdiction of the unit commander in the area, of course. I have noticed that in some cases there are many nights when the armouries are not used. What is the policy of the department with respect to making the armouries available to naval cadets, army cadets or air cadets when they are not being used by the militia in the district concerned? I think everything should be done to assist these other groups and provide this service. There is a janitor on hand at these armouries, and they have to be maintained and heated in the winter at considerable cost.

As the hon. member will know, the various cadet corps are sponsored by local committees, and one of the duties of these committees is to see that the corps have some suitable place in which to meet. However, I think it is fairly generally recognized that at many points there are not suitable places where these cadet corps may meet, except in armouries. The tendency has been-and in my view properly so-to use the armouries for cadet training, when this can be done without interfering with militia training.
Mr. Pallet!: Can the minister tell me how many are on strength in the militia forces of Canada at the present time? How many officers and men are on strength at this time, and how many attended summer camp last summer?

I have not the breakdown as between officers and other ranks, but as
5548	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence of April 20 this year the total effective strength of both officers and men was 45,828, and 16,500 attended camp last year.

I would like to ask a further question about attendance at summer camp. Does the government obtain a reduced rate from the railways for the carrying of reserve militia to summer camps across the country?
Yes, we have a reduced travel rate for military personnel, and this includes members of the militia when on duty.

I have been disappointed that we have had no reply from the minister to statements which have been made, notably by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre in the matter of tanks. I think the only recourse is for me to make a speech on it, myself, which I would like to spare the minister, or to ask him some questions arising out of what was said by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre.
Does the minister agree that in the present state of our equipment and our tactical thinking, in the event of having to put forces in the field the situation would now be that unprotected infantry would be expected to go against machine guns in the field, as happened in the last two wars?

Mr. Chairman, the fact is that we have two armoured regiments of three squadrons each. We have six armoured squadrons which work with our brigade groups. As I said before the dinner adjournment this evening, the composition of the brigade group represents the reasoned result of studies and assessments made by our experts in those fields. I also said we are quite cognizant of the fact that weapons, establishments and formations are changing, and probably will continue to change even more rapidly. Studies are being made of the various arms of the services. A very extensive study is being made of ground forces and the appropriate disposition and size of formations, by NATO, by the United States and by Great Britain, and we are following those studies. We are also making independent studies.
But one does not change policy hastily. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre is the very able exponent of a point of view.
I am not disparaging his point of view, but I do say that what he has said is not the whole story. One must assess the larger picture and correlate the various arms of the services, having in mind their importance. That is- what ; we are endeavouring to do, and what 

we will keep on doing, because there is no finality in these things. They are always changing. However, changes should be evolutionary rather than revolutionary.
I think that is the only way the basic question can be handled. One cannot say, "We are going to scrap all this, and have a lot more of that." One cannot do that unless he is very sure that that is the thing to do.

I do not quarrel with the generalities the minister has just enunciated. Nevertheless what we are asking is that we be allowed to see behind the curtain. I am sure what the minister has said is sensible, and represents the facts as he sees them.
No question of security arises; we are just asking that the curtain be drawn aside so we may be allowed to see what the thinking is. We do not want just to be told that questions are being thought about.
That is why I have been disappointed when the minister appears to content himself with these genei-alities. It would seem that the only way to get information is to ask definite questions. I am not a technician, and it is not an answer to me when the minister makes general references to the brigade groups. I am asking a question bearing on the statement made by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre who, I am sure, is well informed on the subject.
I think the minister can answer that question I asked, because I was staggered today [DOT]-perhaps in my ignorance-when I heard what the situation is. Does he agree that if we had to put a force in the field our infantry might well be in the lamentable position of infantry in the first world war and, I understand, in the second, of having to go unprotected against machine guns? We know the result of that.
I have asked a simple question, and I think I should have an answer to it. What the hon. member said shocked me as I am sure it shocked a lot of other people, and we should have an answer.

I do not know just what the hon. member means by "unprotected". No man is wholly protected in battle. Men could only go into battle with the proper protection in the light of circumstances of today, so far as we know the battle pattern.
I cannot say more than that. No one wants to send troops into action until they are adequately prepared and protected, but there is a great difference of opinion as to what degree there should be of any particular type of protection.
I am not going to express any detailed opinion on these Various matters, because

they are very technical and very serious. I am not going to express any snap view as to whether one type of protection is better than another; because, after all, there is a great deal of technical knowledge involved in the consideration of all these things.
No, no, that is not any good.
Well, that is all I am going to say.
I hope the minister will not stick to that, because I do not think it is fair to do so. He should not treat us like children. These generalities-
And I don't think it is fair to the committee for a member to ask such questions as you are pressing, either. So maybe we will just disagree.

Perhaps we may be able to come nearer together because I think the minister can, if he will, give us a statement of the position which would be satisfactory. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, as I understood him this morning-and the minister may correct me if I am wrong- said that as things stand, we have not undertaken to move all our men in armoured vehicles, and that we would have a considerable number-I do not know how many-who would have to go the old and painfully dangerous way with which we are all familiar.
I think, again, that it is fair to ask the minister-certainly I hope it is-the question I have asked him, and that he ought not to be content, as apparently he has been up to now, merely to tell us that these are problems which are being thought about. We
Supply-National Defence want to know what is being thought about at the moment, because after all they are our problems.
Ten o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Tomorrow we shall begin by considering the suggested changes in the rules. The report being unanimous, it may be that the discussion will not be very long. I should hope it would not be, but in any event we shall not go beyond one o'clock with that discussion. We shall begin in the afternoon with public works and take justice afterwards.

It being four minutes past ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
